name: AshesiGhana
title: Recovering Gold from E-Waste
abstract: Ghana leads Africa in gold production, at visible cost: mercury- and cyanide-based mining has polluted some 60% of its water bodies and stripped roughly 60,000 hectares of land since 2001. Meanwhile Agbogbloshie in Accra holds circuit boards far richer in gold than ore, at 300-400 g per tonne against 5-10 g, burned by hand today. SynMine recovers it biologically. Ground PCBs enter a bioreactor where secreted tetrathionate hydrolase generates thiosulfate, leaching gold into solution; a GolS-based biosensor reports concentration as an efficiency metric; E. coli displaying GolB via an Lpp-OmpA anchor bind Au(I) selectively while copper, nickel, zinc and tin stay in solution; bound gold is eluted with an acid wash and reduced to nanoparticles. We designed, assembled and verified leaching, sensing, recovery and reduction constructs, modelled the full chain, and built the grinder and reactor. Engagement with Agbogbloshie workers, miners and Ghana's EPA shaped each design decision.

name: ASIJ-Tokyo
title: Project 茶(Sa)kure-it-all: Improving the Production of Sakura and Tea-derived Therapeutic Molecules
abstract: As global demand for plant-derived products continues to rise, traditional extraction methods are placing increasing pressure on already vulnerable natural resources. Within Japan, this raises concerns regarding tea supply and sustainable sakura cultivation. While biosynthetic production in yeast offers a promising alternative, current methods remain limited by inefficiency, product build-up inside cells, and cellular stress. This reduces yields and limits large-scale production. Project 茶(Sa)kure-it-all addresses these challenges by engineering yeast to produce the therapeutic compounds sakuranetin, quercetin, L-theanine, and epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) through a dual-strain production model with biosensor flux control, active transport engineering, and optimized growth conditions. These approaches aim to improve production efficiency by creating a scalable and sustainable alternative to plant extraction. By providing a reliable source of bioactive compounds with anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties, our system has the potential to support the needs of Japan's growing elderly population while protecting sakura and tea resources.

name: BGI-College
title: BioH₂: Engineering Microbes for Sustainable Hydrogen Production and Byproduct Valorization
abstract: Hydrogen is a promising clean energy carrier, yet its production remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels. Microbial dark fermentation offers a sustainable alternative, but its potential is constrained by competing metabolic pathways and stringent anaerobic requirements. BioH₂ addresses these challenges by developing Clostridium beijerinckii S63 as an alternative hydrogen-producing chassis. Guided by metabolic modeling, we explored strategies to enhance electron transfer and redirect carbon metabolism. Our engineered strains achieved a hydrogen content of 46.92%, compared with 40.20% in the original strain. Beyond improving hydrogen production, insights from integrated Human Practices and economic analysis encouraged us to rethink the entire production system. We demonstrated that spent fermentation broth could support Bacillus subtilis cultivation, highlighting its potential for value-added microbial biofertilizer production. By integrating metabolic engineering with byproduct valorization, BioH₂ lays the foundation for a circular biomanufacturing platform that aims to make biohydrogen production more resource-efficient, economically viable, and sustainable.

name: BUCT-China
title: Upcycling Food Waste into Sustainable Transparent Material
abstract: CycloGlass introduces a sustainable route to transparent supramolecular materials by combining enzyme engineering, systematic host–guest screening, and bio-based manufacturing. First, we systematically screened dozens of guest molecules and identified L-phenylalanine and L-tryptophan as effective partners for native β-cyclodextrin (β-CD), forming transparent, amorphous films at an optimized host-to-guest molar ratio of 0.8:1. Second, the resulting materials achieved average transmittances of 97.8% and 97.3% across 350–1000 nm, respectively, compared with 18.6% for the control. Third, we established an upstream biomanufacturing strategy using machine-learning-guided CGTase screening, identifying a candidate that achieved 59.0% starch conversion, with β-CD accounting for 45.5% of cyclodextrin products. Combined with fermentation-based production routes for the guest amino acids, CycloGlass demonstrates a pathway toward manufacturing transparent supramolecular materials from renewable feedstocks, including starch-rich food waste.

name: Duesseldorf
title: Cozyme
abstract: Cozyme is a synthetic yeast co-culture system that converts brewery spent grain, an abundant, low-value waste, into high-value compounds like jasmonic acid. Two engineered yeast strains work together, each handling part of the biosynthetic pathway, coordinated through co-culture regulation built with the MoClo Yeast Toolkit. The system is designed to be modular: the same regulatory circuit can be adapted to drive different product pathways, demonstrating flexibility beyond a single target compound. By turning brewery waste into valuable outputs without animal-derived inputs, Cozyme offers a sustainable, circular approach to biomanufacturing, while engaging local breweries and stakeholders through hands-on human practices work.

name: ESSENTIAL KOREA
title: EcoPatch: A Multifunctional Hydrogel Patch for Chronic Wound Care
abstract:
EcoPatch is a biomass-derived hydrogel platform designed to combine reactive oxygen species (ROS) modulation with mechanical deformation monitoring for future chronic wound care.

We expressed recombinant alginate lyases in Escherichia coli and screened alginate degradation products alongside water hyacinth extract. Water hyacinth extract reduced ROS-associated fluorescence in LPS-stimulated RAW 264.7 cells, whereas the tested alginate degradation products showed no significant reduction. These findings guided candidate selection for further development. We also fabricated an alginate–polyacrylamide hydrogel and developed a nanowire sensing prototype for real-time resistance monitoring during deformation.

By combining approaches from synthetic biology, biomass valorization, biomaterials engineering, and biosensing, this work establishes a foundation for developing biomass-derived wound-care materials while highlighting the potential of renewable and underutilized biological resources.

name: GEMS-Taiwan
title: Releaf: A Stress-Responsive Optogenetic Bioreactor for Precision Plant Protection
abstract: Producing the right biological compound, at the right time, at the right amount has traditionally required either expensive infrastructure or constant human oversight. Releaf is a closed-loop biological manufacturing platform built around engineered Bacillus subtilis that couples real-time environmental sensing directly to microbial production. The bacteria manufacture and secrete targeted biological protectants on-site and on-demand, delivered through a membrane for controlled release. The result is a programmable living factory where output tracks need, offering a more adaptive and decentralized approach to biological manufacturing for climate-resilient agriculture.

name: HAMK
title: Regenerative Biofabrication from Agricultural Byproducts (ReFab)
abstract: How can we as humans make materials that behave more like living systems? ReFab explores regenerative biofabrication by studying how agricultural byproducts can be transformed into engineered living materials capable of maintaining viability and recovering from damage. To do so, we recombinantly expressed a protein that could potentially be applied to inactivated mycelial materials and confer self-healing properties. This project investigates a future in which materials are no longer disposable products, but living systems that can persist, adapt, and recover.

name: HangzhouFourteenAP
title: Multi-Enzyme and Antimicrobial Peptide System for Dental Plaque and Calculus Prevention
abstract: Dental plaque and calculus (tartar) are major contributors to oral diseases such as cavities, gingivitis, and periodontitis. Current removal methods rely on mechanical brushing or harsh chemicals, which are often incomplete or inconvenient. Our project engineers a synergistic biological solution combining three enzymes—DNase, protease, and glycosidase—to break down the key components of biofilm matrix (extracellular DNA, proteins, and polysaccharides), thereby dispersing existing plaque and preventing new buildup. Additionally, we design antimicrobial peptides that bind directly to tooth surfaces, inhibiting bacterial reattachment and growth. Together, this system offers a targeted, non-toxic, and easy-to-use approach to reduce plaque accumulation and inhibit calculus formation, promoting long-term oral health.

name: HI-Iceland
title: Making the strongest spider silk UV resistant
abstract: Plastic fibers are prevalent pollutants, harming organisms and entire ecosystems. This creates pressure on biomanufacturers to offer a functional, competitive and environmentally friendly solution. Spider silks are promising as they have recently gained increased attention due to their low density combined with strength and toughness. However, they are challenging and costly in production, and prone to environmental weathering. We therefore had two main goals for our project. Our primary goal was to produce truncated spider silk proteins that originate from Darwin's bark spider, which is known for making the strongest spider silk, in E. coli. Our secondary goal was to explore melanins as UV protective additives to our silk proteins. Our results indicate that the production of at least one silk construct was successful. We did not finish the engineering cycle for the project's UV portion but will continue to work towards it in the future.

name: HK-Joint-School
title: FlaminGone: An Engineered Amyloid Coating for Sustainable Fire Retardancy
abstract: Traditional chemical fire retardants pose severe health and environmental hazards, creating an urgent need for eco-friendly alternatives. FlaminGone delivers a sustainable bio-coating platform using E. coli’s CsgA curli subunit as a self-assembling amyloid scaffold. Fusing hydrophobic BslA for weatherproofing and polyethylene-binding peptides (PEbp) for substrate anchoring, our Two-Layer System (CsgA-PEbp + CsgA-BslA + APP/EG) overcomes secretion limits and steric hindrance. To accelerate construct engineering, we developed PyroForge, a sequence-only machine learning platform using ESM-2 features to predict protein melting temperature, folding free energy, and mutational stability. Under fire testing, the bio-matrix forms a dense char shield that halts flame propagation and self-extinguishes. BslA prevents rain washout across weathering, while Arabidopsis assays confirm zero ecotoxicity. Swapping binding domains extends this platform to diverse industrial materials.

name: HSAS-China
title: BrewZyme
abstract: Coffee shops generate interconnected solid and liquid waste streams. Spent coffee grounds contain valuable chemical components and a material structure that can be repurposed, while residual coffee, milk, and rinse water may promote biofilm formation and odor-related microbial activity. Our project develops a modular coffee-ground utilization platform. We characterize the chemical value of spent coffee grounds and process the remaining material into a reusable scaffold for enzyme immobilization. We load quorum-quenching enzymes onto this scaffold to interfere with bacterial communication in coffee-shop wet waste. AiiA, a characterized AHL lactonase, serves as the first proof of concept for enzyme loading, retained activity, leaching, and reuse. Further more, we characterised AidC, AhlX and QQ-2 as broader extension targeting AHL signalling.

name: IIT Bombay
title: BIFROST: Engineering Yeast to produce Bio-Coolant for Sustainable Data Centre Cooling
abstract:
The growing energy demands of AI data centres have intensified the need for efficient and sustainable cooling technologies. While single-phase immersion cooling can reduce cooling energy consumption, conventional dielectric fluids rely heavily on petrochemical feedstocks and PFA's which pose environmental concerns due to limited biodegradability.

BiFROST aims to develop a bio-based immersion coolant by engineering Saccharomyces cerevisiae to produce medium-chain free fatty acids (FFAs), particularly myristic acid (C14:0). We used PCR-based site-directed mutagenesis to introduce the V1254W mutation in the FAS2 ketoacyl synthase domain of fatty acid synthase, aiming to promote medium-chain fatty acid production. Through metabolic engineering, experimental characterisation, and computational fluid dynamics, we investigate FFA production and the potential of fatty acid-derived fluids for immersion cooling. Future work will focus on introducing in vivo methylation to convert the produced fatty acids into methyl myristate, the target cooling fluid, advancing a renewable route towards more sustainable data centre infrastructure.

name: Jiangnan-China
title: Systematic Engineering of Yarrowia lipolytica for Efficient 7-Dehydrocholesterol Production
abstract: SunForge-713 engineers Yarrowia lipolytica to produce 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC), the precursor of vitamin D₃, from glucose. We combined precursor and sterol pathway reinforcement, intracellular remodeling, and competing-pathway regulation with computationally guided enzyme screening. DHCR24p.(E158H/D436N) achieved 5.82 times the whole-cell 7-DHC titer of the matched wild-type control in a substrate-supplemented assay. Molecular simulations and enzyme-constrained modeling supported interpretation of enzyme behavior and cellular limitations. The final strain, PE13, produced 462.1 mg/L in shake flasks and 4.93 g/L after 120 h in a 5 L bioreactor. Human Practices integrated 311 survey responses with academic and industry consultations to shape evaluation priorities for genetic stability, process robustness, impurity profiles, reproducibility, safety, and downstream costs. A company collaboration agreement established a basis for further technical evaluation. Our project connects strain engineering with stakeholder needs to advance microbial 7-DHC production.

name: KAIST Korea
title: RATAtouille: Multi-Layer Genetic Circuits for Dynamic Metabolic Control
abstract:
In microbial production, performance is decided less by which genes are present than by when they switch on. Static control fixes expression once and holds it for the whole culture, while the cell moves through growth and production. Four costs follow: resources skew to the product and growth slows, intermediates accumulate and inhibit, flux leaks at branch points, and closing a branch collapses growth.

RATAtouille, a Reprogrammable Autoregulatory Transcriptional Architecture, uses what the cell already knows. Input modules reading precursor level, population density and external signals share one output format, so physiological context is read from several angles. Hierarchical logic turns that combination into a single expression state, and the delay through each layer divides the pathway in time.

Our first application is lutein, where one promiscuous cyclase feeds both product and byproduct and cannot be deleted. We change only when it is expressed, so substrate ratio decides the flux.

name: Korea-HS
title: Melano Shield: Engineering E. coli to Produce Melanin-Based Fire-Retardant Coatings
abstract: Wildfires are growing more destructive, and the flame retardants used on wood are halogenated or petroleum-derived. Bio-based alternatives fail on supply, not chemistry: most need plant extraction or synthesis. MelanoShield engineered Escherichia coli BL21 to express a Priestia megaterium tyrosinase under the copper-inducible pCopA promoter, where copper both activates transcription and serves as the enzyme’s cofactor. The strain produced 419 mg of dried pigment per liter, matching a commercial Sepia officinalis melanin standard to within 0.5% in log-linear absorbance slope; an empty-vector control gave none. A two-layer spray coating of the crude cell extract reduced mass loss under 180 s of flame to 3.06 ± 0.73%, against 9.36 ± 1.82% for untreated oak and 3.67 ± 0.73% for a commercial fire protector. At three specimens per condition, we match that product, not beat it, and this is, to our knowledge, the first fire test of a bacterially produced melanin coating.

name: MammothEdu-United
title: BioSonde: Turning Waste PET into Marine-Degradable Radiosonde Shells with Halophilic Halomonas
abstract: Every year, roughly 600,000–950,000 radiosondes are released worldwide and almost none return; their expanded polystyrene shells drift into the sea and fragment into micro- and nanoplastics. Because release is part of the design, the shell material is the only point of control. BioSonde engineers the halophile Halomonas sp. LA5 to convert carbon from waste PET into polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA), a polyester that erodes in seawater, for a foam shell designed to meet China’s radiosonde standard. Three modules build the route: a PETase delivery and expression pipeline in LA5, structure-guided PETase variants stabilised for high salt and temperature, and a ribosome-binding-site library that tunes flux through the PHA pathway. A life-cycle model, with the TPA co-product sold in place of virgin material, shows large carbon savings over conventional PHA production. Interviews with meteorological observatories shaped a four-gate adoption plan, from bench tests to licensed use.

name: McGill
title: LanTurn: Lighting a Path for Mineral Recovery
abstract: Rare earth elements (REEs) are essential for technologies such as electric vehicles, wind turbines, and modern electronics, yet conventional extraction can be environmentally intensive and costly. LanTurn is a platform using Saccharomyces cerevisiae to recover REEs from secondary waste streams. Our system displays lanmodulin (LanM), a protein with high affinity for REEs, on the yeast surface to capture target metals. Using light to control yeast aggregation, we enable cells to clump together for easier collection. By combining selective metal binding with light-controlled recovery, LanTurn aims to complement existing mining processes and integrate into industrial workflows. Our computational model, Luminate, guides LanM protein engineering to improve binding stability and selectivity while evaluating system performance under different conditions and at scale. By transforming waste streams into potential sources of valuable minerals, LanTurn aims to advance a more circular and resource-efficient approach to critical mineral recovery.

name: Mingdao
title: Ethanol from Paper Waste: One-Pot Enzymatic Saccharification and Microbial Fermentation of Plastic-Coated Containers
abstract: Electricity is scarce on the island of Taiwan, yet every school day at Mingdao High School more than 7,000 students throw away paper lunch boxes, coffee cups and ramen bowls whose plastic lining is bonded so tightly to the paper that no ordinary mill can take them back. Most end up in incinerators or landfills — and the energy locked inside them goes up with them. Instead of tearing the plastic off, we unlock the glucose from the cellulose inside the paper. We put shredded containers, a cellulase, a β-glucosidase and Zymomonas mobilis into a single vessel: the enzymes release glucose from the paper, and the bacterium ferments it into ethanol in a one-pot design — simultaneous saccharification and fermentation (SSF). We characterized both enzymes under fermentation-compatible conditions — far from their optimum — modeled the coupling between enzyme and microbe, and built a benchtop fermentor.

name: NBJF
title: ThermoTdT: AI-Engineered TdT for Next-Generation DNA Synthesis and Storage
abstract: With global data booming, traditional silicon - based storage faces issues like high energy use, short lifespan, and low density. DNA storage, with high density, stability, and low energy needs, is a green future option. But DNA synthesis cost and inefficiency hinder it. TdT, a key for enzymatic DNA synthesis, has benefits but poor thermal stability. This study used deep - learning to engineer TdT for better thermal stability. The variants can work stably at higher temps, supporting an efficient, eco - friendly DNA storage system and offering a new data - storage sustainability solution.

name: NFLSHS-CHINA
title: Improving Crocetin production in Escherichia coli through Semi-Rational Engineering of CsCCD2
abstract: Crocetin is saffron’s core active substance with excellent anti-neuroinflammatory, neuroprotective and antioxidant properties, holding great market potential in nutraceutical, cosmetic and pharmaceutical sectors. Traditional plant extraction yields little and costs heavily, making crocetin extremely pricey. Here we use Escherichia coli as a cell factory for crocetin biosynthesis via an eight-gene biosynthetic pathway. We first adopted pET-Duet1 vector to express these genes with dual T7 promoters. Though crocetin was detected in cell factory, low activity of CsCCD2 caused accumulation of zeaxanthin. Using semi-rational protein design, we screened three predicted high-activity CsCCD2 mutants. Wet-lab data confirmed one mutant boosted crocetin yield by 113%. We harvested crocetin-containing powder by freeze-drying bacterial cells and then designed topical soothing essential oil and oral sleep-aid capsules. This work explores a complementary alternative production route for stable, low-cost, green sustainable high-purity crocetin.

name: NJTech-China
title: Symphony in the cell:Biomanufacturing of 5-Hydroxytryptophan via Multi-Scale Engineering
abstract: The global burden of mental health disorders highlight the need for efficient production of bioactive compounds 5-Hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP) due to its outstanding physiological functions in regulating mood and treating depression. Sustainable biomanufacturing of 5-HTP using microbial synthesis offers attractive application prospects. However, it suffers from inherent bottlenecks including low tryptophan hydroxylase activity, inadequate cofactor regeneration, and difficulties in fermentation scale-up. We combined enzyme mining, AI-assisted protein engineering, expression optimization, and model-assisted fermentation to overcome these bottlenecks. Structure-guided design and protein language models generated a TPH7 quadruple mutant with 5.6-fold higher activity than its parent. Reconstructing tetrahydrobiopterin biosynthesis and regeneration enabled 5-HTP production in a tryptophan-producing Escherichia coli chassis. Following optimization of the fermentation contitions, the final engineered strain produced 20.0 g/L 5-HTP in 5 L bioreactor without exogenous tryptophan. This work offers an multi-level regulatory framework and provides reusable tools for synthetic biology.

name: NNU-China
title: Engineered Enzyme System for Green Valorization of Shell Waste and Chitooligosaccharide Production
abstract: Enzymatic production of chitooligosaccharides (COS) often requires elevated temperatures and yields predominantly low-degree-of-polymerization (DP) products. We identified Csn-387, a chitosanase retaining high relative activity across 20–50 °C, and developed a rational engineering strategy guided by structural analysis, substrate-binding modes, and catalytic-pocket interactions. Iterative engineering generated the triple mutant L147W/T229Y/Y263F, shifting the product profile from predominantly DP2–DP3 to DP3–DP6, with DP4–DP5 as the major products. The mutant retained high catalytic activity across 20–40 °C and was further validated in a 100 mL fed-batch hydrolysis system at 24–26 °C without external heating. These results establish a promising biocatalyst for low-energy production of higher-DP COS and a reusable engineering framework for controlling chitosanase product profiles, supporting future valorization of crustacean-processing waste.

name: NNU-Nanjing-China
title: Pigment Green Revolution: Biosynthesis of Indigo from Escherichia coli
abstract: Traditional chemical indigo production produces hazardous waste. This project engineered Escherichia coli for green indigo biosynthesis through multiple strategies. Firstly, we constructed the TnaA-mFMO indigo pathway and obtained an original strain TMF02 with a yield of 0.580 g/L. Then using CRISPR-associated transposase for chromosome multi-copy integration of TnaA and mFMO, the yield reached 1.730 g/L. To overcome the limitations of classic intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), two artificial intelligence (AI) models were developed: PhaseLACE screened the functional natural IDPs and LACE-IDP de novo designed novel unnatural IDPs. A total of 12 candidate condensable IDPs were obtained, and several showed stronger condensation than classic RLP. The top Q97W73-M8 was further applied for the indigo synthesis, resulting in a yield of 3.199 g/L, which was 5.52 times that of the TMF02. This project demonstrated the Innovation of AI in novel IDPs screening and the advantages of artificial membraneless organelles in cell factories construction.

name: NUS-Singapore
title: ORCHID: Observation of Real-time Cellular Health and Intracellular Dynamics for Predictive Biomanufacturing
abstract: In biomanufacturing, achieving economically viable industrial-scale production requires optimization of titre, rate and yield (TRY). However, engineered genetic constructs and heterogeneous environmental conditions often trigger emergent stresses that disrupt cell metabolism and production efficiency. Current methods rely on reactive interventions, adjusting culture conditions or gene expression of biosynthesis pathways after observing impacts of stress, rather than anticipating and preventing these metabolic disruptions. To address this gap, we built ORCHID (Observation of Real-time Cellular Health and Intracellular Dynamics For Predictive Biomanufacturing). ORCHID enables predictive understanding of cellular physiology through modular multiplexed biosensors designed to simultaneously detect multiple intracellular signals. They capture stress responses in real-time across varying culture conditions and gene expression across biosynthetic pathways, linking these cellular dynamics to TRY. To enable predictive biomanufacturing, ORCHID integrates ML/AI to translate the high-dimensional data into predictive insights and actionable strategies, advancing understanding of cellular stress, and ultimately improving biomanufacturing efficiency and robustness.

name: OUC-Haide
title: Carbotex: Weaving Ecological Agri-waste into Valued Ecopolymers
abstract:
Crop straw is abundant biomass with untapped valorization potential. Carbotex innovatively integrates upstream biological saccharification with an engineered Aureobasidium melanogenum A08 cell factory that efficiently converts lignocellulosic hydrolysate into high-molecular-weight poly(malic acid) (PMA), subsequently transformed into high-performance bio-based adhesives.

To address inefficient native xylose metabolism in A. melanogenum A08, we identified and elucidated the roles of the key transcriptional activators AraR and XlnR. Their co-expression significantly improved utilization of mixed hydrolysate sugars and PMA synthesis. Overexpressing a selected pyruvate carboxylase gene further increased precursor supply, enabling a PMA titer of 26 g/L from lignocellulosic hydrolysate. Direct dopamine modification of PMA-containing fermentation broth produced high-strength bio-based adhesives with promising chemical and medical applications.

Carbotex thus links lignocellulose saccharification, hydrolysate valorization, and advanced materials in a closed-loop biomanufacturing pathway, converting agricultural waste into high-value adhesives and offering a reference approach for biomass utilization and carbon neutrality.

name: PSI Korea
title: Bio Color ID: Engineering Biomaterials for Optical Authentication
abstract: Counterfeit products undermine consumer trust across industries, including cosmetics and pharmaceuticals. PSI Korea developed Bio Color ID to explore optical authentication using tags composed of polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) and biopigments. We engineered microbial PHB and indigo production pathways and investigated enzymatic halogenation to expand pigment diversity. We also fabricated PHB tags containing biopigments and measured their RGB responses under five LED illumination conditions and four background colors, generating 60 optical features. Responses varied with pigment composition, loading, and film thickness. Three independently fabricated tags with the same formulation showed consistent profiles. Selected comparisons between visually similar tags and with watercolor imitations on paper revealed differences under specific measurement conditions. Feedback from experts, the public, and industry informed calibration and packaging requirements. These findings connect synthetic biology, material design, and optical measurement, providing a foundation for validating authentication performance using independent samples and assessing future applications to product packaging across diverse industries.

name: RUBochum
title: Cat PURr - Catalytic Polyurethane Recycling
abstract: Polyurethanes (PUR) rank among the most produced plastics globally, yet less than 10% is recycled,the majority is incinerated or landfilled. Chemical recycling via solvolysis recovers polyols but leaves aromatic carbamate byproducts (e.g., MDA-DEG) without viable valorization routes. Our Project Cat PURr aims to close this gap by identifying novel biocatalysts capable of cleaving aromatic carbamate bonds to recover methylenedianiline (MDA), enabling closed-loop recycling. We are Combining sequence- and structure-based enzyme discovery via the Pythia framework, to identify promising candidates for experimental screening. Our goal: expand the enzymatic toolkit for aromatic carbamate cleavage and turn PUR waste into a feedstock for new polymers and fine chemicals.

name: SCU-BSE-China
title: SynAmine: Engineering Yeast for Efficient Polyamine Production
abstract: Spermidine and spermine are high-value polyamines, and their low titre is the main obstacle to producing them in yeast. Improving that titre requires relieving several constraints at once rather than overexpressing a single enzyme, so synthesis was addressed on two levels. Paired transcriptome and proteome analysis of a high-spermidine strain against its parent identified supply steps that had not kept pace with the pathway, and overexpression of MET6 and MET12 raised spermidine 1.20- and 1.12-fold. The terminal step was then strengthened by fusing Spe2 and Spe4 into one polypeptide, tested with six peptide linkers in both domain orders. The forward GGGS fusion produced 214.20 mg/L spermine, 1.8-fold the separate-expression control; the reverse orientation produced 118.41 mg/L, indicating that domain order predominates over linker identity. Thirty-eight parts were registered, comprising the fusion series, linkers, stop-free domains, XII-5 homology arms and nine integration cassettes.

name: SDU-Denmark
title: Shewanode
abstract:
Global energy policy is currently transitioning from fossil-fuel based toward low-carbon, sustainable energy systems. One alternative energy source to conventional batteries that does not require limited resources or produces large amounts of carbon dioxide are microbial fuel cells (MFCs), which use bacteria to convert chemical energy into electrical energy.
Certain bacteria such as Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 can donate electrons to their environment by transporting them through cytochrome complexes in the outer membrane. Additionally, they form outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) carrying the same complexes to enhance extracellular electron transfer (EET).
Our project focuses on improving the naturally found EET by overexpression of the outer membrane cytochrome omcA and complex mtrCAB and destabilizing the outer membrane by deqQ deletion to increase OMV formation for the use in an improved MFC setup to generate electricity. Furthermore, the project aims to establish a better understanding of Shewanella's OMVs through isolating and analyzing them.

name: Squirrel-Guangzhou
title: Cardivit： Engineered E. coli for Salvianic acid A Production and Cardiovascular Protection
abstract: Salvianic Acid A (SAA) from Salvia miltiorrhiza has great value in treating cardio - cerebrovascular diseases and is a key precursor for polyphenolic compounds. Current production by plant extraction has issues like long cycles, low yields, and high costs, unable to meet demand. Our project explores a sustainable biomanufacturing strategy. Using engineered microbial systems, we aim to build a cell factory for stable and scalable SAA production, guided by synthetic biology principles, offering a greener alternative for sustainable pharma manufacturing.

name: SZSAIS-BaoAn
title: From Fermenter to Cold Table: Engineering Microbes for Better Ready Refrigerated Meals
abstract: The refrigerated ready-meal market is growing fast, yet lipid and protein oxidation during processing, cold-chain transport and reheating darkens colour, creates warmed-over off-flavours and reduces water-holding capacity and tenderness. Ergothioneine (EGT), a natural sulfur-containing antioxidant with metal-chelating potential, is a candidate for food quality retention, but low microbial titres have limited its use. We reconstructed an EGT pathway in Escherichia coli, reaching 23.37 mg/L. Testing four SAM-regenerating enzymes, we found ADO1 raised the titre to 39.1 mg/L. Guided by structural analysis, molecular docking and AI-assisted screening, we built six Egt1 single-point variants; K406S performed best, improving the titre by 52.3% over the Egt1/Egt2 baseline. Through consumer surveys, central-kitchen and factory visits and expert interviews, we identified oxidative reddening of high-value peeled shrimp as our first application scenario, and plan to extend biosynthetic EGT to other prepared foods, making cold meals better-tasting and safer.

name: Thailand-XCLASB
title: Melanify, Upcycling PET into Protective Melanin
abstract: PET plastic has become deeply embedded in modern consumer culture, appearing in nearly every aspect of our daily lives. Yet, millions of tonnes of PET plastic still evade recycling each year. The reality is that conventional PET recycling is often inefficient and economically unattractive. Each recycling cycle can degrade polymer quality, limiting how many times the material can be effectively reused before its performance declines. But our solution rewrites the economics: our two host cascade turns consumer plastic into allomelanin, a high-value UV shielding biomaterial. Pichia pastoris secretes a thermostable hydrolase to crack the polymer, glycosylating the enzyme at the same time to increase its thermal stability. The resulting monomers are then utilized by engineered Escherichia coli with surface displays of downstream pathway enzymes to efficiently convert PET derived intermediates into a valuable pigment.

name: Tongji China
title: Virock：Intelligent Microbial Self-Healing Concrete System
abstract: As various infrastructures continue to be built, concrete cracking remains an unavoidable challenge in the engineering field, and conventional repair solutions are not only costly but also fail to deliver long‑lasting repair effects. Perhaps synthetic biology can offer a distinct solution for concrete crack repair! Using Bacillus subtilis as the engineering chassis, this project designs engineered strains capable of expressing mineralization‑assisting proteins to realize biological self‑healing of internal concrete cracks through calcium carbonate deposition. To avoid environmental leakage risks posed by engineered microbes, we have simultaneously devised a biosafety containment system that restricts the survival of engineered bacteria in uncontrolled environments via cell lysis and growth inhibition. We expect this microbial self‑healing system to provide an innovative synthetic‑biology‑based solution for building‑structure protection.

name: TU Delft
title: MOSAIC: MOdular Scaffolds for Adhesive Implant Coatings
abstract:
Medical implants can fail through infection, poor tissue integration and more, causing pain, lost independence and 
repeated treatment for patients. MOSAIC is a biomanufacturing platform powered by synthetic biology which can address these challenges through modular implant coatings made from elastin-like polypeptides (ELPs), engineered proteins inspired by human elastin. We produced and purified ELPs to assess coating performance: surface tests supported attachment, and cell assays showed improved adhesion, spreading and growth. A protease cut the ELP at built-in sites, a route to on-demand drug release, and an antimicrobial peptide inhibited bacterial infections. Our computational models predict how a coating will behave before it is made, while MOSAIC Designer simplifies repetitive gene design and assembly. Stakeholder engagement, production models and regulatory analyses informed a route to scalable biomanufacturing and commercialisation. Together, these advances provide building blocks for multifunctional, personalised implant coatings that could improve the lives of many patients.

name: UCNZ
title: NanoBrew: Transforming brewers' spent grains into high-value nanocellulose
abstract: Brewers’ spent grain (BSG) is a major waste stream from the brewing industry. It is primarily sold as low-value animal feed or landfilled. BSG is a cheap substrate to produce nanocellulose, an emerging material with applications in biomedicine, electronics and packaging. NanoBrew is developing a sustainable, enzyme-oriented approach through recombinant expression of xynA xylanase from 𝘉𝘢𝘤𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘶𝘴 𝘴𝘶𝘣𝘵𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘴 and ancestral Cel5A endoglucanase in 𝘌𝘴𝘤𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘤𝘩𝘪𝘢 𝘤𝘰𝘭𝘪. The xylanase breaks down hemicellulose to increase cellulose accessibility, along with other pre-processing methods. The high-activity ancestral endoglucanase will degrade the cellulose into short fibrils, reducing the processing required to produce nanocellulose. The recombinant enzymes will be secreted out of 𝘌. 𝘤𝘰𝘭𝘪 by fusion to YebF, allowing our process to be more easily upscaled. The economic and sustainable feasibility of a one-pot bioreactor will be assessed using simulations based on our experimental data. We aim to tackle issues in waste management and current nanocellulose production methods.

name: UCS-A
title: Tea to Bioplastic: A Tea-Waste-Driven Microbial Cell Factory for PHB Production
abstract: The rapid growth of the milk tea industry has generated large amounts of tea residue waste, while the widespread use of disposable plastic products continues to intensify environmental pollution. Although tea residues are rich in cellulose and polysaccharides, most are discarded without effective utilization. To address this challenge, we developed a sustainable “Tea-to-Bioplastic” platform that transforms tea waste into biodegradable PHB bioplastics. Through biomass pretreatment, complex polysaccharides in tea residues are converted into fermentable sugars, which are then utilized by metabolically engineered microbes to produce PHB. The resulting bioplastic can be further processed into disposable products such as drinking straws, creating a closed-loop system from tea waste to sustainable consumer goods. By integrating synthetic biology, metabolic engineering, and circular economy principles, our project offers a green solution for waste valorization, plastic reduction, and sustainable biomanufacturing.

name: UCSC
title: AMPiary
abstract: The 2026 UCSC iGEM team presents AMPiary, a streamlined, modular, computationally informed platform for rapidly synthesizing novel antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). We built a standardized AMP expression plasmid and AMPexchange, a method for swapping AMP genes without full reassembly. Engineered E. coli hosts with a dual-mechanism biosafety system produce the peptides. Our machine-learning genetic algorithm, reVAMP, generates candidate AMPs and improves with assay data. We developed this platform to enable Lyme disease research. Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, can progress to antibiotic-unresponsive Post-Treatment Lyme Disease Syndrome. Preliminary studies show honey bee venom AMPs are active against resistant B. burgdorferi, yet no clinical trial has tested them. We developed our AMP manufacturing platform using the sequences for AMPs found in bee venom. We designed, synthesized, purified, and validated apiarin, a novel AMP engineered through AMPexchange. Together, these parts form a modular AMP manufacturing pipeline for developing therapeutic AMPs.

name: UESTC-China
title: E. coli Cell Factory for Itaconic Acid Biosynthesis from Ethylene Glycol
abstract:
Over 400 million tons of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) are produced annually, with less than 10% effectively recycled. Current enzymatic depolymerization strategies primarily target PET breakdown but stop at low-value monomers—particularly ethylene glycol (EG)—which accumulates and inhibits further catalysis. We present UpPlast, a closed-loop upcycling platform that converts PET degradation byproducts into bio-based 3D-printable resins using engineered Escherichia coli.
Our system operates in four stages: (1) EG utilization — we introduced a three syntheti plasmids into E. coli BL21(DE3), enabling EG as the sole carbon source; (2) itaconic acid (IA) biosynthesis — a four-gene module (cadA-acnA-Cg-gltA-Cg-Pyc) diverts carbon flux through the TCA cycle to produce IA at titers significantly above baseline; (3) dimethyl itaconate (DMIC) synthesis — IA is esterified into DMIC, a polymerizable monomer with an intact C=C bond; (4) bio-based resin formulation — DMIC serves as a reactive diluent in UV-curable resins suitable for DLP 3D printing.

name: ULethbridge
title: Utilizing MOSMAGE to engineer optimized microbial chassis for natural compound production
abstract: The scalable production of natural-derived compounds is constrained by low yields and limitations in microbial biosynthesis. To address these challenges, we aim to optimize microbes like Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae, using Multiplex Automated Genome Engineering (MAGE) for natural production biosynthesis. To edit metabolic pathways, we designed the Modular Open-Source Multiplex Automated Genome Engineering (MOSMAGE) platform - a low-cost, modular hardware system designed to automate MAGE workflows. Built from consumer-grade components and customizable modules, MOSMAGE enables high-throughput metabolic engineering through integrated thermal, fluidics, electroporation, and spectrophotometric, systems. To validate the engineering pipeline, we will measure Triacetic acid lactone (TAL) production following genome edits.

name: Ulink-SZ
title: Chitinova: A Crab Shell Upcycling Platform for Joint Health
abstract: Osteoarthritis causes chronic pain and mobility loss for millions of people, while large quantities of shrimp and crab shells are discarded every year. Chitinova aims to address both challenges by developing a green bioconversion platform that transforms chitin-rich shell waste into N-acetylglucosamine (NAG), a bioactive precursor associated with cartilage matrix synthesis. We engineer Escherichia coli to produce and secrete a synergistic enzyme system combining lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases (LPMOs) and chitinases. LPMOs disrupt the crystalline structure of chitin, creating accessible cleavage sites for downstream enzymatic hydrolysis, while chitinases further convert the resulting fragments into NAG. Through enzyme engineering and chassis optimization, we aim to improve catalytic efficiency, stability, and product yield. Chitinova seeks to provide a cleaner alternative to acid hydrolysis while promoting circular use of local seafood-shell waste and supporting future joint-health applications.

name: UniCRETE
title: RHAea
abstract: RHAea is iGEM uniCRETE’s 2026 project idea, dedicated to valorizing Olive Mill Wastewater (OMWW), a toxic by-product of two-phase olive oil production in Crete, by mitigating its environmental impact while unlocking its industrial potential through three distinct outputs. In Stage 1, a chimeric protein (CBM3–linker–HyT12) anchored on bacterial cellulose selectively captures hydroxytyrosol, the waste's most abundant phenolic antioxidant, which holds significant value for the cosmetic, food, and pharmaceutical industries. In Stage 2, an engineered, non-pathogenic strain of Pseudomonas putida utilizes the detoxified waste's remaining organic load to biosynthesize eco-friendly rhamnolipids for green detergents. Finally, in Stage 3, we aimed to test whether the treated water is validated for circular reuse as nutrient-rich fertigation water in local olive groves.

name: VGA-Pinion
title: AstraEV
abstract:
Chronic UV exposure drives reactive oxygen species accumulation in skin, causing oxidative damage and photoaging. Cells defend themselves through the KEAP1–NRF2–ARE axis, where NRF2 is released under stress and switches on protective genes such as HMOX1/HO-1. Many antioxidants can engage this axis in principle, but poor stability and limited penetration keep them from reaching the cells that need them. Vesicle delivery is a promising answer, yet mammalian-derived exosomes face cost and regulatory acceptance.

Astragalus-EX asks whether plant-derived exosome-like vesicles can serve as that platform instead. We isolate vesicles from Astragalus membranaceus (Huang Qi) and pursue two cargo strategies against the same pathway: quercetin in HaCaT keratinocytes as an epidermal model, and siKeap1 in NIH/3T3 fibroblasts as a dermal model. Two computational models — one kinetic, one spatial — help us locate the limiting step and prioritize experiments.

name: Worldshaper-Nanjing
title: MUSCLE-SHIELD: A Green Biomanufacturing Platform for L-Carnosine to Support Sarcopenia Intervention
abstract: As global aging deepens, sarcopenia has emerged as an overlooked crisis that strips the elderly of their independence through progressive muscle loss, while sustainable access to supportive nutrients remains limited. We plan to engineers E. coli as a green cell factory for L-carnosine production. By optimizing metabolic pathways, we aim to improve substrate uptake, product export, and biosynthetic yield. Our project seeks to provide a low-cost, sustainable L-carnosine supply for future nutritional strategies supporting sarcopenia intervention and healthy aging.

name: YCYW-China
title: BioCapsule Delivery Platform
abstract: Our project aims to develop a pH-responsive capsule for targeted enzyme delivery to help manage lactose intolerance. The capsule is designed using carboxylated lignin and cellulose, with citric acid serving as a crosslinking agent to support polymerization and glycerol to improve flexibility. To introduce pH-responsive properties, we explored lignin modification using a laccase–TEMPO oxidation system to introduce carboxyl groups into lignin. Although we produced recombinant laccase, the yield was insufficient for subsequent experiments. Therefore, commercially available laccase was used for lignin modification. The modified lignin was then characterises using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) to evaluate changes in its functional groups and support further capsule development.

name: YHA-HWFLA
title: Fel d1 Eraser: A Pet‑Friendly Neutralizing Spray That Enzymatically Degrades the Cat Allergen Fel d1
abstract: As allergic reactions triggered by the cat allergen Fel d 1 become increasingly common, existing management strategies generally suffer from limitations such as incomplete degradation, poor safety, and difficulty in large-scale application, which greatly hinder the harmonious coexistence between allergic individuals and their pets. We aim to construct a safe, efficient, and precisely controllable Fel d 1 degradation system, complete product development tailored to practical scenarios. Using synthetic biology approaches, we achieve precise optogenetic regulation of enzyme activity, ultimately forming a product format consisting of a light-protective spray paired with a portable blue light activator. This study not only provides a safe pathway for heterologous expression of proteases, establishes standardized synthetic biology components, and expands the application scenarios of light-controlled enzyme systems, but also addresses the root cause of cat allergy symptoms, promotes harmonious human–pet coexistence, and offers a new paradigm for the management of pet allergies.

name: YNU-China
title: Engineered RBC-membrane platform for mitochondrial delivery
abstract:
Mitochondrial dysfunction underlies numerous diseases, yet delivering intact mitochondria to target cells remains challenging. Free mitochondria lose membrane potential rapidly and distribute non-specifically without a directing signal.
We engineered a mitochondrial capsule consisting of a mitochondrial core enclosed within a DMSO-induced MEL erythroid membrane hybridized with a defined artificial-lipid layer. A hypotonic swelling–loading–resealing strategy solved the key encapsulation barrier, achieving reproducible high-efficiency loading. Screening seven lipid formulations identified Formulation 2 (CHOL/DOPC/POPC/LPC/DSPE-PEG2K) as optimal. Replacing DSPE-PEG2K with DSPE-PEG2000-mannose generated a targeting variant for CD206 macrophage mannose receptor-mediated uptake. Uptake was assessed in RAW264.7 macrophages versus NIH/3T3 controls using a mito-GFP reporter as a dye-independent readout. The entire system uses murine Risk Group 1 cell lines at BSL-1, providing a reproducible, tunable foundation for mitochondrial delivery research.

name: Yucai-SZ
title: SpotAway
abstract: Oil stains—composite stains of grease carrying hydrophobic pigments like capsanthin deep into fabric fibers—resist conventional surfactant- or oxidant-based removers, which require water and scrubbing. We designed SpotAway, a dry-activatable, portable bio-enzyme emergency stain patch. Stored as a free-water-free porous xerogel with trehalose–mannitol lyoprotectants, it activates in situ with just 1–2 drops of water. Its functional layer employs a dual fusion-protein system: a CBM–capsanthin-binder fusion that specifically captures hydrophobic pigments, and a triolein-binding domain–lipase fusion that anchors oil droplets at the oil–water interface and degrades triglycerides. Computationally, we built a pipeline combining structural screening with docking-based binding pre-evaluation; experimentally, four Design–Build–Test–Learn cycles delivered validated candidate binders and modular Binder–lipase fusion exploration. SpotAway offers a portable, targeted, gentle solution—stopping stains, and embarrassment, at the very first moment.

name: ZJU-China
title: Native-like programmablE cartilage Scaffold for Tissue repair (NEST)
abstract: Cartilage regeneration has long stood as one of the defining challenges of regenerative medicine: true repair requires rebuilding a load-bearing microenvironment where mechanics, anisotropic architecture, and biochemical signals act together. NEST, a native-like programmable engineered cartilage scaffold for tissue repair, uses synthetic biology to manufacture a biomimetic hydrogel that recreates this native logic from molecule to material. Its silk-elastin-like protein backbone is rationally designed to tune mechanical strength, crosslinking behavior, and tissue compatibility, while functional peptide modules introduce cartilage-oriented capabilities such as magnetic alignment, glycosaminoglycan retention, and inflammation-responsive cargo release. A modular ligation system enables these functions to be flexibly assembled and exchanged, tailoring the scaffold to patient-specific needs and diverse clinical conditions. By aligning molecular design with tissue-level function, NEST moves beyond replacing damaged cartilage toward restoring the biological principles that sustain it, envisioning biomaterials as dynamic microenvironments that help tissues recover their native form and function.

name: Austin-UTexas
title: RAD to the Future
abstract: Deinococcus radiodurans is a highly resilient bacterium capable of surviving ionizing radiation, severe desiccation, and extensive DNA damage, making it a promising chassis for synthetic biology in harsh environments such as space and hazardous waste sites. Our project aims to make D. radiodurans easier to engineer by expanding its genetic toolkit. We developed new parts and adapted existing parts for Golden Gate Assembly to improve modularity and standardization. We also explored TnpB, a compact Cas9-like system derived from mobile genetic elements, as a potential method to improve homologous recombination in the polyploid D. radiodurans genome. Additionally, we developed a modular gene repression system using catalytically inactive TnpB (dTnpB) and explored its potential for future predictive modeling. Together, these approaches expand the genetic tools available for engineering D. radiodurans and help lower barriers to using this resilient organism in synthetic biology.

name: Bologna
title: PHAGED-IT: PHage Assissted Gene EDiting
abstract: Gene editing can rewrite DNA precisely, but it cannot choose which cell to enter. Because surface markers can be shared between pathological and healthy tissue, single-receptor targeting is not selective enough. PHAGED-IT addresses this issue with two engineered M13 bacteriophages that split the editing system between them: one, retargeted to EGFR, carries a the guide RNA; the other, retargeted to FRα, carries the Cas9-derived base editor. Neither edits alone, so the cell surface itself becomes a molecular AND-gate and editing occurs only where both receptors are present. We are building the system in parts. Our cell models, HEK293 and MDA-MB-231GFP, are established and their transfection optimized; several base editor and guide RNA combinations have been tested; our first phages have been produced and purified, and the EGFR and FRα targeting components are in preparation. The architecture is modular: changing the receptors aims the same platform at different cells.

name: CalPolySLO
title: Synthetic Cells: An Accessible Platform for Education and Engineering
abstract: Synthetic biology and cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) offer alternatives to engineering biology in living cells, but cost and technical complexity often keep these platforms out of undergraduate hands. Our team developed a modular enzyme-characterization toolkit and undergraduate curriculum that make cell-free and synthetic-cell systems accessible to non-experts. CHEM 471, “Engineering Synthetic Cells,” teaches synthetic-biology skills while using student outcomes to refine the platform and educational materials. We extended this work to Cold Spring Harbor’s Synthetic Biology Program, contributing protocols, hardware, and training. Our measurement toolkit centers on class III polyphosphate kinases (PPK2s), which regenerate nucleotide triphosphates from NDPs and NMPs. Its real-time assay measures consumption of multiple substrates to classify new PPK2s and characterize enzyme kinetics. PPK2-driven NTP regeneration strengthens cell-free systems as an alternative platform to living cells. Low-cost emulsion hardware enables reproducible synthetic-cell production in classrooms. Open designs, protocols, and data give future iGEM teams a reusable framework.

name: Claremont CA
title: Phagenomics
abstract: Phage therapy's bottleneck is host range: each phage binds a specific receptor on a specific strain, so matching phage to target means screening, not design. We isolated our own system from soil at the California Botanic Garden: Pseudomonas capeferrum and an unnamed relative in the Pseudomonas putida group, with their co-occurring phages. Phage Phi8 is novel: 62,339 bp, 80 CDS, no database match, no virulence or resistance genes. Modelling then redirected the project. Structure prediction and protein language models showed the recognition step is not protein-protein: the receptor-binding apparatus is branched, and one accessory protein is a depolymerase degrading the bacterial polysaccharide layer. The key interaction is protein-sugar. We therefore asked whether ancestral depolymerases were more generalist, reconstructing ancestors of the phage's GH5 glycoside hydrolase, scoring them with an enzyme-conditioned language model, and expressing modern and ancestral enzymes in E. coli, reporting what worked and what did not.

name: Columbia NYC
title: Project SENTINEL
abstract: Stroke remains a leading cause of disability and death worldwide, with therapeutic efficacy declining rapidly post-onset. Although circulating biomarkers offer early diagnosis, the design of high-affinity biosensing binders remains constrained by the opacity of generative protein models. These models operate as black boxes, which obscures the features that drive high affinity and specificity. SENTINEL addresses this bottleneck by introducing a mechanistically-interpretable framework for de novo protein binder engineering. By integrating Sparse Autoencoders with ESM-based protein models, we extract human-interpretable features associated with molecular recognition to steer towards high-affinity binding. We benchmark SENTINEL against leading design architectures and, as proof-of-concept, validate candidate binder pairs for clinically relevant stroke biomarkers (UCH-L1, VILIP-1, and B-FABP) through split reporter survival assays. Through coupling resolved AI design principles and synthetic biology, SENTINEL aims to establish mechanistic interpretability as a universal accelerant for rational protein binder design—adaptable to any disease where early detection saves lives.

name: Concordia-Montreal
title: BiblioTK: Engineering a Gram-Positive Toolkit System
abstract: Across different iGEM projects, the BiblioTK team noticed a clear trend: Gram-negative bacteria dominate, favoured for their well-characterised nature and familiarity.  Their Gram-positive counterparts, however, remain underutilised despite strong and relevant applications. To bridge this gap, we are expanding the existing Gram-positive genetic engineering platform, SubtiToolKit (STK), by developing functional tools for other under-researched strains. Our approach centres around two new modular parts: Part E, providing modular origins of replication as independently exchangeable components within STK’s Golden Gate grammar and pGRAMLIN, a split-marker shuttle vector that couples antibiotic selection to correct recircularisation, improving transformation efficiency in Gram-positive hosts. Alongside the wet-lab, we developed Project Bookmark, a statistical analysis tool that identifies candidate promoter regions across bacterial sequences, streamlining genetic part discovery. Together, these tools make established Gram-positive chassis for synthetic biology and biomanufacturing, extending a shareable, cross-species-transferable parts standard to organisms with therapeutic and industrial promise beyond traditional model organisms.

name: Duke
title: PACERS: Refining PACE with RNA Switch Control
abstract: Phage Assisted Continuous Evolution (PACE) accelerates protein engineering by linking protein activity to bacteriophage propagation. However, leaky expression of the infectivity protein pIII can reduce host cell susceptibility to infection and allow suboptimal variants to propagate. To address this challenge, Duke iGEM developed PACERS (Phage Assisted Continuous Evolution with RNA Switch), a strategy incorporating RNA toehold switches to regulate pIII translation. These synthetic RNA structures repress translation without a trigger RNA and activate it when the trigger is present. By placing the toehold switch upstream of gene III and encoding its trigger sequence in the selection phage, PACERS aims to minimize unintended pIII production while enabling activation following infection. With this controlled expression system, PACERS has the potential to improve continuous protein evolution reliability and support applications in medicine, agriculture, and biotechnology.

name: DUT-China
title: SHUFFLE: Self-iterative High-throughput Unlocked Flexible Frequency Loci Editor
abstract: Improving microbial cell factories requires precise, diverse mutations across multiple loci, yet conventional genome-editing methods are limited by insufficient targeting control, restricted substitution spectra, or double-strand-break toxicity. We developed SHUFFLE (Self-iterative High-throughput Unlocked Flexible Frequency Loci Editor), a targeted N-to-N base-editing platform combining dual-activity TadDE, Cas9 nickase, and paired guide RNAs. Iterative engineering expanded PAM recognition with nSpCas9-NG, incorporated AlkA and CWBEmini modules, and evolved TadDE using EvolvePro to obtain A158R. The optimized TadDE_A158R–nSpCas9_NG–AlkA editor achieved up to approximately 50% editing efficiency at tested loci and generated diverse nucleotide substitutions. SHUFFLE enabled diversification of global regulators to identify strains with improved growth and polyhydroxybutyrate production on ethanol, and editing of the accA ribosome-binding site to improve malonyl-CoA availability, as indicated by flaviolin screening. SHUFFLE provides a versatile approach to targeted diversification for microbial strain engineering.

name: ETH-Zurich
title: preCISe: modular and targeted protein delivery into mammalian cells using extracellular contractile injection systems
abstract: Protein therapeutics offer unique advantages as inhibitors and enzymes, making them promising candidates for treating a wide range of diseases. However, their inability to efficiently cross cell membranes generally limits their access to intracellular targets. preCISe addresses this challenge with a platform for target-specific protein delivery based on extracellular contractile injection systems (eCISs), bacterial nanosyringes that inject cargo directly into the cytosol. The platform comprises a modular eCIS design that can be retargeted to new receptors by exchanging their binding domains, preCISion reporter cell lines that quantify intracellular delivery, and our deCISion software which finds cell-specific receptors and binders and returns ready-to-order DNA sequences. Because receptors unique to one cell type are rare, we initiated a dual-targeting strategy: the cargo is split between two eCISs addressing two receptors and reassembles only in cells displaying both. Our software OpenSplitProtein ranks split sites that preserve folding and spontaneous reassembly.

name: Evry-Paris-Saclay
title: ORBIT - Orthogonal Ribosome Bioengineering Iterative Toolbox
abstract:
The ribosome builds every protein in every living cell and it is one of the hardest machines in biology to engineer - a change that suits an engineered purpose usually cripples the host. Orthogonal ribosomes sidestep this by reading only their own messages. ORBIT set out to establish the system that can evolve it.

Three advances had never been combined: a tethered ribosome whose subunits cannot swap with native ones, an evolved 16S rRNA that translates faster and the cleanest orthogonal binding-site pair described. We built every combination - 16 ribosome plasmids and nine reporters, all sequence-verified and obtained E. coli strains surviving solely on tethered ribosomes. The improvements do not transfer between architectures, so a tethered ribosome must be evolved on its own terms. 

ORBIT delivers a characterized toolkit for tethered-ribosome evolution: strains, parts, readouts, software and a clear account of what each of them does.

name: Example
title: Best year yet
abstract: Maybe this is our year?

name: FHS-China
title: ProLac: Characterization of a Probiotic and In Silico Optimize Lactose Consumption for Lactose Intolerance Relief
abstract: Lactose intolerance is a highly prevalent digestive disorder. Over 90% of adults in Asia lose lactase persistence, and many of these people suffer from symptomatic lactose intolerance. Distinct from previous iGEM teams that aimed to construct new engineered strains, we launched ProLac, an observation-first synthetic biology project. We characterized an acid- and oxygen-tolerant probiotic *Lacticaseibacillus paracasei* subsp. paracasei CICC 6109 with growth curve assays and plasmids sequence analysis. With COBRApy, we performed in silico *manM* knockout simulation on *Lacticaseibacillus paracasei* ATCC 334 based on a published genome-scale metabolic model to redirect carbon metabolism for preferential lactose utilization. To address the wet-lab experimental challenges, we managed to develop a multifunctional fluorometer. We also built an open-source tool for campus biology map for science outreach and released our campus map as a demo.

name: Fudan
title: GlycoGarden: A Programmable Platform for Glycoengineering
abstract: Glycans are essential biomolecules involved in protein function, immune recognition, and disease, yet they remain difficult to study and engineer because their biosynthesis is non-template-based, heterogeneous, and highly dependent on intracellular localization. GlycoGarden aims to bridge this gap by developing a yeast-based synthetic biology platform for programmable glycoengineering, in which engineered intracellular glycosylation pathways are rationally rewired to produce defined, controllable glycan outputs on yeast surfaces. Based on this platform, GlycoGarden facilitates glycosylation mechanism studies, cancer-associated glycoantigen therapy development, high-throughput screening of glycan-binding molecules, and production of glycan-based bioingredients for biomedical and food-related applications. Ultimately, GlycoGarden seeks to establish a modular synthetic biology platform that makes glycan research and glycoengineering, with long-term public value.

name: GTIIT-China
title: Self-Exciting Quantum Dots: Bioluminescence-Driven Excitation of Yeast-Biosynthesised CdSe
abstract: Quantum dots are bright fluorophores whose colour is set by particle size, but they need an external light source, which also excites the surroundings. We built a quantum-dot system that excites itself. The yeast Yarrowia lipolytica was engineered to synthesise cadmium selenide inside the cell from selenite and cadmium salts, and to express a fusion of the CdSe-binding peptide CdSeBP to NanoLuc luciferase. Supplied with furimazine, NanoLuc emits blue light and transfers energy to the bound particle, which then emits in the red without illumination. Absorption spectroscopy tracked cadmium sulfide formation, fluorescence spectroscopy compared selenium and cadmium combinations, peptide binding was measured in vitro, and confocal microscopy showed that emission originates inside cells and requires both precursors. Finally, an extra copy of MET25, a selenium-pathway gene, raised particle emission several-fold. Biosynthesised quantum dots can therefore be excited by an enzyme rather than by a lamp.

name: Heidelberg
title: VOYAGE: Programmable Gas Vesicles for Acoustic Observation and Organization
abstract: We present VOYAGE, a modular platform that enables gas vesicles to become a programmable interface between ultrasound and synthetic biology. These genetically encoded protein nanostructures scatter acoustic waves and collapse at defined pressures, enabling their use for measuring and manipulating cells. We engineered gas vesicle variants for multiplexed in vivo imaging and coupled enzyme activity and the presence of soluble biomarkers to acoustic signals. Beyond observation, our toolbox enables precise spatial organization, and sorting of distinct cell types. Our computational model, ATLAS, built alongside experimental data, unites simulation, generative protein design, and deep-learning image analysis into a framework. Inside and outside the lab, our Fail Forward initiative builds an open culture around setbacks in science through education and by addressing challenges at both individual and systemic levels. Uniting our toolbox, computational modeling, and a culture of learning from failure, VOYAGE transforms how we explore, understand, and engineer biology using acoustics.

name: HKUST
title: Developing a promoter toolkit for Clostridium butyricum
abstract: Out team aims to develop a set of reliable, standardized promoters for Clostridium butyricum. Ultimately, we want to contribute to the broader characterization of C. butyricum. Human practices runs alongside these efforts, providing feedback that directly informs our design, shapes how we communicate risks and benefits, and guides our education initiatives.

name: HongKong-PuiChing
title: Conditional Localized Assembly of Synthetic Proteins (CLASP)
abstract:
Within living cells, functions arise from conditional spatial assembly of molecules. Synthetic biology enables gene-expression editing, yet post-translational spatial control remains limited by chemical or light methods that leak and lack geometric precision.

CLASP (Conditional Localized Assembly of Synthetic Proteins) overcomes this with a modular scaffold using a rigid CTPR backbone, customizable sensors, payloads, split-luciferase reporting, and optional covalent locking. It enables programmable nanometer-precision proximity: recruit, report, retain, and react in response to chosen signals.

ORIGAMI, a physics-based active-learning tool, models structure-proximity relationships to guide closed-loop CLASP design.

CLASP can be applied in salinity-responsive enzyme assembly and biomarker diagnostics as it is a universal, geometrically programmable platform that turns induced proximity into deliberate engineering.

name: IITKGP
title: dSyPhER: dynamic Synthetic Phosphorylation via Effector Response
abstract: Chronic inflammation and the lack of precise, tunable control over cell signaling remain key challenges in engineering therapeutic cell systems. DySPHER (Dynamic Synthetic Phosphorylation via Effector Response) addresses this using modular synthetic receptors in HEK293T cells that convert extracellular TNFα and rapalog binding into programmable, ligand-specific phosphorylation cascades. By coupling receptor dimerization to PUmHD-zipper interactions and IRES-eIF4E-mediated translational control, our platform enables precise, user-defined activation of gene expression, offering a generalizable framework for sensing disease-relevant and chemically inducible signals and translating them into controllable cellular outputs, with applications in inflammation biosensing and cell-based therapeutics. Guided by extensive stakeholder engagement, school and community outreach, and a clear entrepreneurship roadmap, DySPHER reflects our commitment to science that is both technically rigorous and grounded in real-world relevance and responsibility.

name: Imperial College
title: reGELerate - structured, functionalised, prion hydrogels
abstract: The goal of our project was to develop a tunable biomaterial where protein fibrils are treated as discrete mechanical struts as opposed to a tangled aggregate. Non-infectious prions and amyloids have long been used by iGEM teams in everything from bio-wires to gene switches but we chose to focus on HET-s from Podospora Anserina which is an attractive biomaterials candidate due its lack of structural polymorphism. Alongside our wet lab work we produced dry lab modelling for every step using in silico construct design, molecular dynamics and aggregation modelling. Alongside our human practices interviews we chose to focus specifically on biosecurity and bioethics producing frameworks examining how our work intersects with diverse stakeholders. We hope these resources could also be applied more broadly for future synthetic biology innovations. Finally, through our education campaign we engaged every level of society from primary school up to experienced scientists.

name: JLU-CP
title: DigiCAT：A Multi-Threshold Biosensor for Monitoring of Feline Diabetic Ketoacidosis
abstract: Converting continuous molecular signals into programmable genetic decisions remains a challenge in synthetic biology. We developed a modular multi-threshold biosensing platform using β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), a biomarker associated with feline diabetic ketoacidosis, as a proof of concept. BDH converts BHB into acetoacetate (AcAc), which is sensed by the AtoSC two-component system to regulate the expression of Bxb1 and phiC31 integrases. By tuning integrase expression through ribosome-binding sites (RBSs) and integrating mathematical modeling to guide threshold design, our system aims to convert continuous molecular inputs into discrete genetic states and fluorescent outputs. This work provides a modular framework for programmable multi-threshold biosensing.

name: Keio-Japan
title: One Direction
abstract: The development of intercellular adhesion technologies that enable the formation of specific topologies is essential for advancing synthetic multicellular systems. However, existing cell adhesion platforms have primarily focused on controlling the selectivity of cell-cell adhesion, without achieving control over the spatial orientation of cells. In this project, we aim to develop a foundational technology that enables the design of cell orientation in multicellular systems. We propose a genetic design that localizes adhesion machinery to both poles of rod-shaped Escherichia coli, enabling control over the spatial orientation of adhering cells.

name: KIT
title: ENCORE: Engineered Nanocompartments for Capture, Optimization and Reactor Engineering
abstract: No standardized cloning system previously existed for expressing programmable protein nanocompartments, encapsulins, together with customizable cargo in a eukaryotic host. To address this, we developed the ENCORE toolKIT: a Golden Gate-based, modular cloning system for combining encapsulins, cargo proteins, targeting peptides, linkers, and promoters in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Built on a domesticated shuttle vector, the toolKIT organizes parts into five-part cassettes across a three-level cloning hierarchy. We extended the yeast MoClo standard by splitting its single coding sequence position into separate modules, so that shells, targeting peptides, linkers and cargo can be exchanged independently rather than cloned anew for every combination. To support accessible construct design, we developed ENCORE Builder, a web-based software tool for in silico construct planning. We demonstrate the platform through a nanoreactor enabling oxygen-free biocatalysis, the confinement of a hydrogen peroxide-dependent enzyme cascade, and an mRNA capture system preserving transcriptomic snapshots of stress responses for retrospective analysis.

name: Leiden
title: Vascular Engineered Self-assembling Scaffold for Living Organoids)
abstract: Testing new drugs and treatments in reliable preclinical models is an essential step before they reach patients. Commonly used models, however, do not fully reflect how human tissues behave. Organoids offer a promising alternative because they form more complex and mature structures, and represent human biology more accurately than traditional models. Organoids face one major limitation: the lack of blood vessels (vascularization). With VESSL, we aim to address the challenge of vascularization by developing a peptide-based scaffold to support the formation of vascular-like structures in 3D bioprinted organoids. We designed peptides that self-assemble into fibres, forming a network that endothelial cells can attach to and migrate along. Through computational modeling, we assessed different designs to identify candidates predicted to form stable coiled-coil structures and efficiently self-assemble. Five promising peptide candidates were then selected for production using the bacterium E. coli, the fungus Aspergillus niger, and cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS).

name: Marburg
title: CLiPPR - A Toolbox for Flexible, Inducible Gene Expression in Chloroplasts
abstract:
Plants account for around 99% of Earth's new biomass. Through photosynthesis they convert light, water and CO₂ into valuable biomolecules, possibly making them the cheapest biofactories we have. Yet for biocompound production we almost always reach for microbes; not for plants, and least of all their chloroplasts.
Chloroplasts combine photosynthesis with high-level recombinant protein production. But growth and production compete, limiting yield. In microbes, dynamic control decouples the two; currently equivalent chloroplast tools are limited. Plants themselves offer a solution: they regulate chloroplast gene expression post-transcriptionally via nuclear-encoded RNA-binding proteins.

We introduce CLiPPR (Chloroplast Library for Inducible PPRs), a modular toolbox for on-demand control of chloroplast gene expression. Synthetic Pentatricopeptide Repeat proteins (PPRs) bind engineered 5'-untranslated regions placed upstream of any gene of interest, while nuclear inducible promoters provide temporal control over PPR production.

Testing in cell-free extracts, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and Nicotiana benthamiana, CLiPPR aims to advance resilient chloroplast-based production.

name: Munich
title: Primetheus
abstract: While nuclear genome engineering has advanced rapidly, mitochondrial gene editing remains fundamentally unexplored, current methods being limited to specific single nucleotide substitutions. Prime editing is a gene editing system consisting of a Cas nickase fused to a reverse transcriptase (RT) and a prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA) used as a template to synthesize a new, edited strand without introducing double-strand DNA breaks. Our project Primetheus adapts this system for mitochondria through separate import of the fused Cas-RT complex and the pegRNA into mitochondria. To overcome the technical challenge of verifying intra-mitochondrial RNA delivery, we are also developing a novel, genetically encoded RNA-based readout system to enable continuous live-cell RNA monitoring. Primetheus will enable researchers to introduce a wider range of edits, including all base substitutions, as well as longer insertions into mitochondrial DNA, allowing in-depth studies of the mitochondrial genome and unlocking new therapeutic approaches.

name: NAU-CHINA
title: CellApp: Compartmentalization via Engineered Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation for Achieving Programmable Protein Regulation
abstract: Synthetic biology has long sought to improve metabolic efficiency through compartmentalization, yet engineering dynamic and reversible compartments in prokaryotes remains a major challenge. Traditional rigid protein scaffolds often impair enzyme activity and lack orthogonal control. To address these challenges, our project developed a tunable dynamic membrane-less organelle toolbox in E. coli based on liquid-liquid phase separation. Specifically, we designed several orthogonal modules that respectively enable long-term static sequestration, reversible condensation in response to rapid light-controlled aggregation, temperature and pH, and intein-mediated repeated enzyme swapping. These modules collectively provide programmable, reversible and orthogonal control of compartmentalization.
