Our toolbox offers a versatile platform for regulation in synthetic biology, promoting efficient biomanufacturing.

name: NUDT-CHINA
title: Ubik: Programming Degradation with AI-Designed Ubiquitin Codes
abstract: Cells naturally dispose of unwanted proteins by tagging them with a "destroy me" signal called ubiquitin. Targeted protein degradation tries to hijack this system to eliminate disease-causing proteins, but current methods like PROTACs are limited because they must recruit a handful of natural E3 ligases, cellular machines that attach the ubiquitin tag, leading to a shortage of suitable drug targets, poor drug-like properties, and unpredictable tissue effects. We take a different approach: instead of recruiting natural E3 ligases, we use AI to design entirely new, programmable “ubiquitin codes”, miniature artificial modules that directly catalyze the ubiquitin tagging of any chosen disease protein. By creating these synthetic degradation signals from scratch, we bypass the E3 bottleneck entirely, making the system more predictable, more broadly applicable, and more drug-oriented. This transforms targeted protein degradation from a hunt for natural E3 ligands into a programmable, AI driven engineering discipline.

name: Patras-Med
title: ICHNOS: Trace the Invisible
abstract:
Every cell has a history that its present state may not reveal. As transient stress responses fade, information about their intensity and timing becomes difficult to recover, complicating assessments of experimental reliability and reproducibility.
ICHNOS addresses this challenge through a modular synthetic biology platform in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, combining stress-responsive sensing, a TetR-based circuit and a tandem fluorescent timer. ICHNOS-Vail, our software tool application, analyses fluorescence signals through image analysis and mathematical modelling to estimate past stress events.
At the heart of our project lies modularity: interchangeable sensing elements connect different biological inputs to a shared processing and reporting architecture. This design, combined with insights from stakeholder discussions, led us to explore potential future applications in the fields of biomanufacturing, cosmetics, food and nutrition and agriculture.
Together, ICHNOS and ICHNOS-Vail provide a foundation for adaptable cellular recording, helping researchers investigate both a cell’s current state and the experiences that shaped it.

name: Princeton
title: SymPleco: Engineering a High-Surface-Area, Light-Regenerable, Bio-Safe Phage Platform for Precision Toxin Sequestration
abstract: SymPleco is a precision sequestration toolkit that opens the door to novel cancer therapeutics, a last-line-of-defense cure for neurological diseases, and safe environmental bioremediation for the world’s waterways. We modified the M13 bacteriophage chassis to support orthogonal sortase ligation of proteins for molecular sequestration. Combined with our software SymPlify, which designs high-affinity de novo binder proteins for globular proteins and small molecules, the SymPleco toolkit provides a foundational advance in building tunable capture technologies for any target. Our functionalized phages also proved to be ingested and digested by murine bone marrow-derived macrophages, allowing for their biosafe removal. Our immediate future direction of incorporating photo-switchable opto-monobody domains will introduce light‑dependent affinity changes, allowing renewable release without chemical elution. Altogether, we built a novel, highly programmable, scalable yet specific sequestration platform pivotal to environmental and medical remediation that bridges the intractable trade-off between capacity and specificity in current adsorption technologies.

name: Queens-Canada
title: MOSAIC: A Modular Operator System for AND-gated Input Coupling in engineered Escherichia coli
abstract: Engineered bacterial biosensors enable programmable detection of molecular signals, with applications across healthcare, technology, and environmental monitoring. Yet many existing systems remain constrained to single-target detection and application-specific designs, limiting their adaptability where cellular context is dictated by multiple stimuli. MOSAIC is a proof of concept architecture for constructing customizable dual-input biosensors in E. coli, integrating pairs of interchangeable two-component regulatory systems (TCSs) with a genetic AND logic gate. In silico and in vitro work provide foundational data for characterizing individual parts and their integration into functional biosensors, supporting a modular toolkit of three functional layers: wild-type and variant TCSs for sensing, split T7 RNA polymerase for signal integration, and a choice of reporter modules for measurable output. We present a standardized and flexible framework for engineering dual-input AND-gate biosensors in E. coli, enabling interchangeable sensing architectures that can be adapted and expanded by future iGEM teams and researchers.

name: Rice
title: DigiActivate: Chemically Induced, Tunable Gene Activation
abstract: Cell fate is governed by fluctuations in gene expression over time, yet CRISPR transcriptional tools are binary, holding a gene ON or OFF at a fixed level over a fixed period. Engineering that timing and magnitude is what therapies for haploinsufficiency or T cell exhaustion require. DigiActivate achieves this by fusing an array of inducer gated switches onto dCas9, where each switch controls the recruitment of a different transcriptional activator. We tested multiple levels of activation on a two switch array through flow cytometry, where we observed distinct 1.3, 1.7 and 1.9 fold increases in eGFP mean fluorescence intensity corresponding to inducer additions of B, A and A+B respectively. Finally, we used RFdiffusion to design compact de novo binders replacing the natural, bulky E3 ligase domains. The result is a modular part collection in which the inducer or the effector can be changed by swapping a single part.

name: ShanghaiTech-China
title: MOSAIC: Modular Orthogonal Stochastic Automated Integrated Consortia
abstract: MOSAIC is a genetic toolkit for constructing multicellular communities with diverse cell states and tunable population ratios. It uses Cre-lox recombination to generate different DNA configurations and Bxb1-att recombination to convert them into distinct cellular states. These communities are measured through reporter signals and evaluated using our hardware and software workflow to identify suitable population compositions. Once a desired ratio is selected, the reporter system can be switched to functional outputs, allowing different cell types to cooperate in research, medical, and industrial applications.

name: TAU-Israel
title: CERNAL: Compiler-like Engine for RNA-based Logic
abstract: Synthetic biology aims to program cells to sense and respond to various signals; however, we currently lack a universal framework that allows these conditional actions to be easily programmed. Since cells already respond to environmental and internal changes through shifts in their gene expression, harnessing that into actionable inputs enables enhanced programming. To achieve this, we present CERNAL: a computational platform that transforms transcriptomic data into universal, RNA-based logic circuits. CERNAL is a computational compiler designed to evaluate differential gene expression profiles and construct RNA-based logic circuits. The CERNAL pipeline identifies specific genes to act as inputs, computes the corresponding logic gates (e.g., toehold switches and CRISPR sgRNAs switches), assembles potential circuit architectures, and outputs the optimal configuration based on predictive modeling. We demonstrate the versatility and entrepreneurial viability of the CERNAL platform through validation of two applications: a prokaryotic PFAS biosensor and a therapeutic strategy for eukaryotic Endometriosis.

name: Tianjin
title: Genome Revival
abstract: Genome Revival asks whether a yeast genome can regain independent growth through temporary support from another cell. We explored protoplast fusion and developed a genetic route using Saccharomyces eubayanus spores lacking the essential gene CDC15. Mating with Saccharomyces cerevisiae provided temporary support. We then restored CDC15 and used HAnDy-derived tools to remove the helper chromosomes. Parental-marker PCR, whole-genome sequencing coverage and growth assays supported recovery of the S. eubayanus lineage. The sealing-wax system combines red colony colour with a DNA watermark for lineage identification. We organised chromosome-elimination components into the CENSOR Collection and developed the Genome Revival Toolkit for DNA design. Public engagement and comment analysis shaped our communication and ethical reflection, leading to SBTI, an interactive exploration of bioethical perspectives. Together, these efforts connect experimental genome revival with reusable tools and public discussion.

name: Toulouse-INSA-UT
title: CHIRALYS: Aptamers through the looking glass
abstract: Our team iGEM Toulouse has designed next-generation DNA aptamers to bind proteins, pathogens or cancer cells with unprecedented stability. Current aptamers built from “right-handed” nucleotides, the natural chirality found in biology, are prone to degradation in the human body and in a physiological environment. We propose to create mirror-image, “left-handed” aptamers that will evade natural degradation mechanisms, enhancing their long-term binding capabilities. We devised experimental and in silico strategies to design, produce, and characterize mirror aptamers targeting peptides and proteins. Moreover, we engaged in the debate about the risks and ethical issues of creating a “mirror life”.

name: Tsinghua
title: NucleArk—— A Nuclear Delivery System Based on Phase-Separating Condensates
abstract: Efficient nuclear delivery into slowly dividing cells remains a major challenge, particularly for large nucleic acids such as plasmids. Yet, many such cells—including retinal cells, cardiomyocytes, and neurons—are critical therapeutic targets in the human body. This delivery bottleneck has significantly hindered genetic therapies targeting these cell types. By leveraging the high biocompatibility, low biotoxicity, and efficient cargo encapsulation capacity of phase-separated droplets, we aim to establish a safe and effective platform for plasmid nuclear delivery.

name: TU-Dresden
title: MOCHI - Making OCH1 Controlled Humanization Inducible
abstract: We use a tool called RNA interference (RNAi), a natural mechanism for regulating gene expression, that lowers the production of the targeted gene’s protein by repressing the translation of the complementary mRNA. Our work builds upon the work of Ruan et. al. (2025) that showed that RNAi can be established in Komagataella phaffii when the Argonaut 1 enzyme from Naumovozyma castelli is introduced together with a double stranded RNA (dsRNA) precursor. This publication points out a limitation: the silencing might weaken over time. Our proposed solution is creating a stronger dsRNA signal by introducing an RNA dependent RNA polymerase that constantly supplies new dsRNA molecules. We want to achieve this by introducing QDE-1 ΔN from Neurospora crassa. The result we hypothesize to be more templates for further silencing and the creation of a self-enhancing loop.

name: USTC
title: TEMPO: Timed Expression and Suicide Module with Programmable Oscillator-Coupled Binary Counter
abstract: Biological functions depend not only on what cells do, but also on when they act. Many existing genetic timing strategies couple timekeeping directly to a specific downstream function, so adapting them to a new task often requires redesigning the timing circuit itself. TEMPO instead separates timekeeping from execution, providing a modular internal clock that can connect to different downstream programs. It integrates three modules: an oscillator-based CLOCK that produces periodic internal signals, a reversible MEMORY that records successive signals as binary DNA states, and an ACTUATOR that links selected counts to specific outputs. Binary encoding enables multiple stages to be represented without adding a complete regulatory layer for every new step. By tuning the clock period, target count, and output gene, the architecture provides a general framework for staged biomanufacturing, sequential research perturbations, timed therapeutic programs, and programmed elimination for biocontainment.

name: UTDallas
title: SPARC (Signal Protease Amplification Reaction Cascade)
abstract: Both natural and synthetic genetic circuits amplify inputs through gene expression, whereas protein-based circuits promise faster response times than genetic circuits. We constructed SPARC, a synthetic protein circuit that uses a series of synthetic proteases to rapidly amplify input signals and produce custom secreted protein outputs. First, we engineered the SPARC input module by using rapamycin-activated proteases. The activated protease then cascades to activate another synthetic protease using antiparallel coiled coils, which can be reconstituted only upon proteolytic cleavage. To complete SPARC with a custom output module, we engineered protein secretion using secreted embryonic alkaline phosphatase (SEAP) that can be activated by the protease cascade module. Combining these modules will establish a foundation for a fast, programmable cell signaling pathway at the protein level.

name: Utrecht
title: EVerse - Reaching Beyond Biological Barriers
abstract: Biological barriers protect our organs from harmful substances, yet they can also prevent medicines from reaching the tissues that need them. EVerse explores a way around this delivery problem using extracellular vesicles (EVs) and aims to provide researchers with a ready-to-use, non-immunogenic vehicle that can be easily modulated to target and endocytose any cell in the body. An EV-associated scaffold protein presents a SpyCatcher on the surface of the vesicle, which can be conjugated to a SpyTag-equipped nanobody. By exchanging nanobodies, it is possible for the vesicle to recognise different receptors and proteins without rebuilding the entire carrier. We chose the blood-brain barrier (BBB) as our proof of concept to validate the engineered system through cell-based characterisation, transwell assays, and zebrafish embryos. These experiments are an early test of the platform's design and capabilities, with further work needed to establish reliable transport and functional cargo delivery.

name: Vilnius-Lithuania
title: BMClick: One Shell to Click Them All
abstract: Cells provide organisation at the cost of control, and test tubes offer precise conditions but lack order. Neither approach keeps pace with what we ask of biomolecules in today’s rapidly advancing scientific world. Confronted by this problem, we drew inspiration from bacterial microcompartments (BMCs), aiming to bring a part of cellular organisation to the tube. By modifying a single BMC component - the trimer - we were not only able to create a microscopic box capable of encapsulating and displaying novel cargo, but also an environment where that cargo is protected. And if a shell is not what one needs, the trimer can be converted into a functional material that holds cargo on an open surface, be it active enzymes or even whole microorganisms. All these options define BMClick as a modular toolbox that can find its purpose in industry, therapy, and fundamental science.

name: Virginia
title: ChronoContain
abstract: Engineered organisms are increasingly being deployed outside the laboratory setting, creating biosafety risks if they remain or spread in an open environment. Current biocontainment systems often rely on environmental triggers, which can fail under changing real-world conditions. Needed is a biological device that enables controllable and predictably timed cell death, allowing cells to function normally for a defined time before autonomously activating a lethal lysis mechanism. Our solution to this problem is a modular, time-controlled genetic kill switch that enables predictable and autonomous activation of cell death after a defined period of time. We are engineering a modular timed kill switch in E. coli that leverages bacteriophage-derived holin-antiholin systems to enable precisely timed cell lysis. Our controllable timed lysis system provides predictable, autonomous containment, enabling safer deployment of engineered microbes. Our timed self-lysis system is a foundational advance that will enhance the opportunities for deployment of synthetic biology devices.

name: Washington
title: HedgehogSense: A Platform for Tuning Ciliary Receptor Abundance
abstract:
The Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway plays an essential role in embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, and cell differentiation. Dysregulation of this pathway is associated with developmental disorders and several cancers. A key component of Hedgehog Sinaling, Smoothened (SMO), is regulated by the MGRN1–MEGF8–MOSMO (MMM) complex, which controls SMO ubiquitination.

HedgehogSense aims to engineer a modular platform for controlling ciliary receptor abundance by repurposing and disrupting endogenous regulatory machinery. Our system explores two complementary approaches: first, we use chemically induced dimerization to recruit the E3 ubiquitin ligase MGRN1 to SMO, with the long-term goal of extending this recruitment strategy to other ciliary membrane receptors. Second, we are developing a reproducible computational protein design pipeline to engineer miniprotein disruptors that interfere with endogenous MMM complex interactions, providing an opposing mechanism to prevent overdegradation. Ultimately, HedgehogSense seeks to move beyond SMO-specific regulation toward a modular platform capable of tuning ciliary receptor abundance.

name: WHU-China
title: Differphase
abstract: Differphase is a synthetic biology platform for programmable cellular differentiation through liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS)-mediated asymmetric plasmid partitioning. Founder cells establish polarized intracellular organization via LLPS and engineered c-di-GMP signaling gradients, biasing plasmid segregation during division to generate distinct cell lineages through intermediate buffer states. Orthogonal plasmid partitioning systems (ParB/parS and SopB/sopC) enable irreversible lineage diversification by physically separating genetic modules, while a light-responsive dedifferentiation module partially restores the founder state to maintain long-term population stability. Coupled with a toxin–antitoxin stability module, Differphase provides a modular framework for engineering dynamic, self-maintaining multicellular behaviors in bacteria. By overcoming key limitations of conventional co-culture systems, it offers a generalizable strategy with potential applications in tumor-targeted therapies, programmed microbial consortia for biomanufacturing, environmental remediation, plastic-degrading biofilms, and distributed multicellular logic systems.

name: William-and-Mary
title: BRO[K]EN: Building Resilient Optimized Engineered Networks
abstract: Synthetic biology has enormous potential to address real-world challenges, however engineered biological systems must do more than work initially: they must work reliably and safely over time. Like all engineered systems, genetic circuits can break. Mutations, selection, burden, and environmental stresses can compromise function. Systematic failure analysis are not yet routine across synthetic biology, particularly in realistic operating environments. To address this challenge,  William_and_Mary  iGEM  developed BROKEN: Building Resilient Optimized Engineered Networks, bringing failure-analysis principles from mature engineering disciplines into synthetic biology. Our project integrates three goals: DETECT, MITIGATE, and PREDICT circuit failure. We performed longitudinal experiments on four engineered circuits in laboratory and simulated environmental conditions; developed mathematical and machine-learning approaches; engineered detection and prevention systems; and used multitiered functional and molecular measurements to investigate deterioration. BROKEN seeks to move synthetic biology beyond circuits that work initially toward systems that remain predictable, dependable, and safe throughout their intended use.

name: XJTLU-China
title: dogmaOS: Translation-Folding Control for Protein Expression in Escherichia coli
abstract: From recombinant insulin to modern biopharmaceuticals, prokaryotes have been widely used for protein production due to their low cost, rapid growth, and mature genetic toolkits. However, many eukaryotic proteins remain difficult to express in soluble and functional forms in prokaryotes, as differences in translation dynamics and cellular environments can affect protein folding. To address this challenge, we introduced dogmaOS, a programmable translation operating system built in E. coli. It explores codon optimization and tRNA pool engineering as a co-design problem, enabling programmable control of translation and protein folding. Our model integrates promoter activity, tRNA availability, elongation rate, and co-translational folding into a unified framework to guide coding sequence design. Based on model predictions, dogmaOS tunes elongation dynamics to better match protein folding requirements. By treating translation as a programmable biological operating system, dogmaOS enables precise control over protein synthesis, opening new possibilities for controllable protein production in prokaryotes.

name: XMU-China
title: STING: Small TnpB-based Innovative Nuclease toolkit for bacterial Genome editing
abstract: STING develops a compact bacterial genome-editing toolkit based on ISHahl1 TnpB. The system achieved gene deletion in E. coli (4.2–100%) and P. putida (30–44%), alongside transcriptional repression and cytosine base editing. Structure-guided evolution expanded recognition to five noncanonical TAMs. Computational modelling integrated Protenix, Gaussian-mixture scoring, and molecular dynamics simulations to optimize TAM recognition. Integrated Human Practices incorporated expert and stakeholder feedback to improve functionality and biosafety. A self-targeting biocontainment circuit reduced bacterial survival by up to five orders of magnitude. Core parts include ISHahl1 TnpB (BBa_26F4MI62), programmable reRNA, inactive TnpB variants, and base-editing modules, establishing a versatile miniature genome-engineering platform.

name: Al-Nahrain-IRAQ
title: SYNOVA: AI-Guided Prediction of Yeast Fermentation for Bioethanol from Iraqi Date Palm Waste
abstract: SYNOVA (Synthetic Yeast Next-generation Organism Valorization Application) is a software platform, four apps in all, that helps a team decide what to test for bioethanol production by Saccharomyces cerevisiae from Iraqi date waste, a sugar-rich residue now mostly discarded. Instead of trial and error, SYNOVA combines a kinetic model of one batch fermentation (Engine 1, not yet shown to predict real batches), a ranking of genes that changed in RNA-seq experiments (Engine 2), strain comparison across 17 published conditions, and tools for a lab's own measurements (Lab Data). The wet lab used a species-specific PCR workflow to identify local yeast isolates; RT-qPCR of shortlisted genes is the next step. We ran workshops for children, students and the public, and consulted agricultural, business and AI specialists, whose feedback changed what we built.SYNOVA: Helping Choose Strains and Conditions to Test for Bioethanol from Iraqi Date Waste

name: BostonU
title: Cirrus: Creation and Optimization of Cloud Laboratories for Synbio
abstract: Many synthetic biology researchers could benefit from a high-throughput, remotely accessible cloud lab. However, there is no standard or organized method for integrating cloud accessibility into the synthetic biology lab space. We created Cirrus to support both new and existing labs in their transition to optimized cloud labs. Users specify a target and maximum budget, identify the equipment they own, define their laboratory space within an interactive sandbox, select the protocols they wish to run, and indicate the weekly frequency of each protocol. Users may also prioritize either maintaining proximity between related equipment or minimizing walking distance. From these inputs, Cirrus generates a build-ready cloud lab blueprint. Each custom plan comprises a curated bill of materials, standardized protocols, an optimized floor plan, and a cloud lab interface for workflow management. Implementing Cirrus will allow your lab to become a node in a network of remotely accessible cloud labs.

name: Denmark-GA
title: ECLIPSE - Evaporatively Cooled LOCKR Integration for Peptide Screening & Evaluation
abstract: Designing a functional peptide binder for LOCKR, a programmable protein-switch platform, requires extensive GPU usage and months of wet-lab experimentation, since most design software predicts candidates without a level of accuracy needed for evaluating functionality. Malaria illustrates why this limitation matters. Current diagnostic tests target a gene subject to deletion, resulting in 2 in 10 cases going undiagnosed. This is a deficiency the WHO has formally acknowledged, and closing that gap requires a faster, more reliable design pipeline. Our tool, LATTE, meets this need by analyzing binders for LOCKR, through charge scanning and thermodynamic modelling. Our scoring function, HybridDock-Pep complements it, rapidly evaluating protein-peptide binding affinities and selectivity. These tools produce ECLIPSE, a PfLDH-based malaria diagnostic, demonstrating a scalable, computation-first approach to protein diagnostic design, applicable wherever speed and accuracy determine outcomes in many diseases.

name: DKU
title: PeptiCraft: AI-Powered Multifunctional Fusion Protein Design Platform for Skincare and Medical Aesthetics
abstract: Skincare and medical aesthetics present needs for multifunctional biomaterials. We built PeptiCraft, an AI-powered web platform that proposes recombinant fusion proteins based on users’ chosen product formats and functions, together with recommended expression strategies. Refined over iterations, the pipeline screens 849 million public protein sequences through 9 filtering rounds, with safety applied as a hard veto. Negative controls help assess screening performance. The deployed platform supports screening within a 20.2-million-peptide search space and provides 496 precomputed candidate constructs across four functional directions. As a proof of concept, we tested an antioxidant silk-fibroin construct for a topical moisturizer. Preliminary antioxidant and cell-based assays supported initial feasibility and informed model improvement. Our Human Practices work explored societal needs and ethical questions around beauty and AI through outreach and communication. Together, these efforts support computational design and early-stage evaluation of multifunctional protein biomaterials.

name: EdgeSci-THU-China
title: (E)vidence-driven (Co)-administration (P)redictive Analysis for (I)nvestigational New Drugs
abstract: ECoPI is an AI-Agent system for evidence-driven predictive analysis of co-administration risks involving investigational new drugs. By coordinating specialized agents for pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, toxicology, and patient education, ECoPI transforms biomedical evidence into interpretable mechanism–effect–risk chains. The system provides early warnings for researchers and accessible safety explanations for patients.

name: NEBS-VCA
title: Mechanism-Guided PETase Engineering for Environment-Aware Polyester Recycling
abstract:
Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) persists in waste streams because enzymatic breakdown is limited by polymer accessibility and catalytic performance. We investigated FAST-PETase using two complementary engineering routes: structure-aware mutation discovery and active-site-focused design. PET-film assays identified Y87Q and S187Y as beneficial variants, while molecular dynamics, pre-reaction-state analysis, and quantum chemistry helped explain their different effects on catalytic geometry and reaction energetics.
Building on these results, we present an environment-aware design strategy informed by EnzOracle, a framework for predicting enzyme melting temperature, optimal catalytic temperature, and optimal pH. Studies of photoprotective PET-based copolyesters and chemically recyclable polyethylene-like polyesters provide material-design context and suggest future enzyme–substrate compatibility experiments. These extensions remain to be directly validated.
Our project highlights how experimental evidence and mechanistic interpretation can guide more reproducible PET hydrolase engineering.

name: NJU-China
title: Starase Atlas
abstract: Discovering enzymes for specific reactions remains challenging, as protein sequence space is vast and known enzyme–reaction relationships are incomplete. To address this, NJU-China 2026 developed ATLAS, integrating COMPASS, a reaction-guided AI agent; BRIDGE, a protein retrieval model; and EDGE, a graph-based knowledge base of enzyme–reaction relationships. From a user-defined reaction, COMPASS uses BRIDGE to search broad protein space, apply taxonomic constraints, and combine functional, structural, mechanistic, and enzyme-family evidence to prioritize candidates, while EDGE stores and visualizes validated knowledge. To evaluate ATLAS, we applied it to the conversion of farnesyl diphosphate to β-farnesene. The top-ranked candidate, UniProt protein M5AW86, previously unannotated with this activity, was experimentally confirmed to catalyze the reaction, revealing a new enzyme function. Through iterative prediction, validation, and inclusion, ATLAS progressively expands the metabolic knowledge network and enables interpretable enzyme discovery for synthetic biology.

name: SJTU-Software
title: Owl-Eyezyme
abstract: Finding natural enzymes for target reactions is challenging because databases and prediction tools are fragmented, and results are difficult to reproduce. Owl-Eyezyme is a multi-agent virtual laboratory that transforms a reaction description into a ranked, traceable shortlist of enzyme candidates. Large language models coordinate a principal investigator, four domain specialists, a scientific critic, and a reporter to plan tasks, operate bioinformatics tools, evaluate evidence, and summarize findings. The platform integrates reaction classification, protein retrieval, structural analysis, and enzyme–reaction matching through flexible research workflows and reproducible fixed pipelines. Staged execution and checkpoints support limited computing resources, while recorded inputs, intermediate results, failures, and uncertainties preserve the evidence chain. Owl-Eyezyme supports candidate selection and experimental planning, helping researchers move from chemical targets toward laboratory validation.

name: Tsinghua-A
title: mRNA Vaccines for Feline Immunocastration: An AI-Driven Platform from Sequence to Application
abstract:
mRNA technologies offer programmable biological expression, but sequence performance remains difficult to optimize. Existing RNA language models and translation predictors can score candidates, yet many do not generate and iteratively refine host-adapted designs, while cross-species transfer remains uncertain. Using feline GnRH immunocontraception as a case study, we developed an AI-assisted platform for mRNA optimization.
For 5′UTRs, we implemented an ERNIE-RNA-guided hybrid genetic algorithm and an Optimus-based directed-mutation route. For CDSs, our exploration progressed from a conditional VAE, through an interpretable multi-objective genetic algorithm, to a DiT-based structure-aware Refiner that preserves proteins while learning patterns from natural sequences. We integrated these methods into RNA Optimization Studio, a local CPU application supporting validation, five workflows, whole-construct assembly, ranking, visualization, and export.
Representative UTR runs increased mean predicted MRL by 33.1% and 42.8%. Reporter measurements revealed both useful signals and remaining uncertainty, establishing a foundation for future wet-lab-guided optimization.

name: USP-Brazil
title: S(H)ARP - Streptomyces Hidden Antibiotic Regulated Pathways
abstract: The global dissemination of multidrug-resistant pathogens listed by the World Health Organization poses a major public health challenge and highlights the need for investment in the research and development of new therapies. Actinobacteria are widely recognized for their ability to produce secondary metabolites; however, most of their Biosynthetic Gene Clusters remain silent under laboratory conditions. To accelerate the discovery of novel antibiotics, we aim to integrate synthetic biology and bioinformatics approaches to uncover new pathways for the production of bioactive compounds. Our project is structured around three complementary pillars. First, we are developing a bioinformatics tool for the semi-automated identification of novel BGCs in actinobacterial genomes. Second, we are constructing a modular Golden Gate-compatible cloning system for Streptomyces spp., to be used for the first time in iGEM. Finally, through our Human Practices initiative, we will engage the public in the search for novel actinobacteria across different regions of Brazil.

name: XJTLU-Software
title: AMPilot
abstract: AMPilot is an AI-powered research workbench that helps users develop antimicrobial peptides from an initial idea to experimental planning. Users describe their goals and requirements in natural language, and AMPilot searches relevant literature, generates candidate sequences, and evaluates their properties, predicted activity, and potential safety concerns. It helps researchers compare candidates, explore formulation and production options, and prepare editable reports and experimental handoff materials. Throughout the workflow, evidence sources and prediction limitations remain visible, while key decisions stay with the researcher. By bringing these tasks into one workspace, AMPilot helps users organize complex research and prepare for laboratory validation.

name: AEI Prep-Taiwan
title: synPETic
abstract: Plastic waste is a growing burden on manned spacecraft. The ISS, for example, produces about 2,500 kg of plastic waste per year, and resupply costs $10,000–$20,000 per kilogram. Additionally, traditional industrial PET recycling methods require temperatures of 240–285 °C and use metal catalysts, neither of which are currently feasible in space. SynPETic engineers a PETosome, a scaffold-based two-enzyme system produced by engineered E. coli, to depolymerize PET at 37–50 °C. We expressed and purified three functional proteins and measured PET film depolymerization by HPLC. Our human practices include expert consultations and a community survey on attitudes toward GMO-based recycling. For entrepreneurship, we have outlined a pre-commercial pathway serving space agencies, commercial station operators, and remote Earth sites, monetized through development contracts, pilot services, and licensing. Our process is compatible with biological repolymerization. Our unique contributions include a new composite part and reusable measurement protocols.

name: AFMU-China
title: NEXO: Engineered Exosome-Producing Microneedle Patches for Microgravity-Induced Muscle Atrophy
abstract: Long-duration spaceflight poses challenges for maintaining skeletal muscle and supplying repeated treatments. NEXO explores a living-cell microneedle platform for sustained delivery of engineered exosomes. We engineered HEK-293T cells with modules for SMAD7 mRNA loading, skeletal-muscle targeting, and enhanced exosome production, and encapsulated them in layered GelMA microneedles. Under simulated microgravity, experiments supported increased exosome yield and sustained encapsulated-cell viability; co-culture studies provided initial evidence of reduced myotube atrophy. Models investigated nutrient supply, secretion dynamics, molecular interactions, and tissue exposure to inform design and further validation. Our modular Registry collection and interactive modeling resources support adaptation by other teams. Stakeholder engagement shaped usability, safety, and research-ethics priorities, while education activities developed reusable resources through participant feedback. NEXO remains an in vitro prototype: in vivo delivery, containment, long-term safety, and performance in actual spaceflight require further investigation.

name: Barcelona-UB
title: Guard’s Up: A temporary, reversible and non-integrative genetic protection against space radiation
abstract:
As humankind prepares to conquer the stars, radiation remains one of the greatest challenges to long-duration human spaceflight. Current protection strategies rely mainly on physical shielding, heavy and limmited against high-energy cosmic radiation. 

Synthetic biology offers an alternative: engineering cells to better withstand radiation-induced DNA damage. The Guard’s Up system combines the tardigrade-derived Damage Suppressor Protein (Dsup) with a DNA targeting system to provide broad DNA protection while reinforcing selected radiation-sensitive genomic regions. 

The system is maintained episomally, without any modification of the genome, and can be switched off and progressively cleared once it isn’t needed simply by taking a doxycycline pill. By combining targeted protection with temporary, non-integrative genetic engineering, Guard’s Up aims to provide an additional layer of cellular radioprotection for safer long-duration human space exploration.

name: BGCFullerton
title: MycoVela: Protecting Mycorrhizal Fungi for Future Space Agriculture
abstract: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) can improve plant nutrient acquisition and stress tolerance, but oxidative stress associated with lunar regolith may reduce fungal viability and disrupt plant-fungal symbiosis. MycoVela is a project designing a cell-free antioxidant carrier system designed to protect Rhizophagus irregularis spores and hyphae during early exposure to lunar regolith simulant. The formulation uses pyomelanin produced through heterologous HPPD expression in Escherichia coli, which is recovered and incorporated into a protective carrier near AMF propagules. We also designed a novel catalase optimized for activity in regolith. The deliverables can even be applied here on Earth, as improved AMF symbiosis has the potential to increase the yield for many crops. Proposed experiments test the catalase root-zone treatment and compare pyomelanin-containing carriers with ascorbic acid, carrier-only, and stress-only controls while measuring spore viability, hyphal growth, and oxidative-stress response. This work aims to improve AMF resilience in lunar-regolith-based plant growth systems.

name: BIT-LIFE
title: Mars Magnet
abstract: Iron monitoring matters in space; detection stays in the lab. BIT-LIFE (iGEM 2026) asked: what if the detector were alive? On E. coli's Fur switch, three tracks close one loop. Trained on 112,955 promoters, a CNN screener (P@20 = 1.00) and CNN–Transformer scorer (R² = 0.5684) narrowed 51,203 candidates to 25. Five designed promoters drove Cycle3GFP across 0–30 µM iron; S3 and S5 fell over 0–10 and 0–15 µM. A sealed pocket detector takes it off the bench.

name: BNDS-China
title: OrbitColi
abstract: During long-term space missions like Artemis, astronauts are exposed to cosmic radiation and microgravity, leading to oxidative stress that conventional antioxidant supplements have limited efficacy due to instability and fixed dosing. We designed OrbitColi, an engineered Escherichia coli probiotic platform that detects and mitigates oxidative stress in the astronauts’ gut. It senses glycochenodeoxycholic acid (GCDCA), a biomarker indicating food intake, and an oxidative-stress-responsive signal, with both inputs integrated through a split T7 RNA polymerase AND gate to ensure responses only occur when both conditions are present. Its activation triggers the production of trehalose, protecting proteins against oxidative damage, and riboflavin (vitamin B2), supporting detoxification of reactive oxygen species. To enhance storage and deployment, the engineered probiotics are designed to be freeze-dried, improving shelf life and stability for on-demand use.

name: BUCT
title: Air2Protein: Turning Martian Air into Programmable Nutrition
abstract: Air2Protein is a modular electro-biocatalytic platform that converts Martian atmospheric resources into microbial protein and functional nutrition precursors. Since the Martian atmosphere is rich in CO₂ and contains exploitable N₂, we first transform CO₂ into a concentrated formate/formic acid feedstock through electrocatalysis, while establishing ammonia as a controlled nitrogen input and evaluating N₂-to-NH₃ conversion as a long-term nitrogen-supply module. These inputs are then integrated with an engineered E. coli chassis carrying the reductive glycine pathway, enabling formate-derived one-carbon units to enter central metabolism and support single-cell protein accumulation. By further redirecting carbon flux toward amino acid biosynthesis and installing a β-alanine branch for L-carnosine production, Air2Protein demonstrates a programmable route from atmospheric gases to both basic biomass and functional nutritional ingredients. Designed for Mars but relevant to Earth, this system proposes a scalable, closed-loop strategy for food production in extreme, resource-limited environments.

name: EPFL
title: OrbitAl
abstract:
Every year, hundreds of satellites burn up on re-entry, releasing their metals into the stratosphere. Spacecraft are built largely of aluminium, so re-entry injects aluminium into a layer of the atmosphere that normally receives almost none; pollution that is essentially unmonitored. What matters is not only how much metal comes back down, but the form it takes in the aerosol particles that carry it, since that form decides whether living systems can take it up.
Orbit-AL has two components. The hardware is a balloon-borne sampler that captures stratospheric aerosols and keeps them intact and uncontaminated until they reach the lab. The biology then reads those samples: for aluminium, a protein we designed to fold around Al³⁺, an ion with no natural biological sensor; for iron, engineered Escherichia coli reporters that distinguish ferric (Fe³⁺) from ferrous (Fe²⁺) iron. Mass spectrometry quantifies the same samples, giving the biological signal a chemical reference.

name: HAS
title: AstroFlora: Solutions for Plant Growth in Microgravity
abstract: Growing plants in space is essential for controlled ecological life support systems, as plants provide food, oxygen, and purified water, absorb carbon dioxide, improve the environment, and alleviate psychological stress for astronauts, while also laying the groundwork for lunar and Martian settlements. However, microgravity disrupts normal plant growth, partly through excessive accumulation of abscisic acid (ABA) and indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) in roots. Here, we designed a plant probiotic system based on engineered E. coli that reduces this excessive hormonal accumulation in plant roots under microgravity conditions, enabling normal plant growth despite microgravity stress. We also developed a hardware system, Floraspin, that facilitates laboratory simulation of plant growth under microgravity conditions, and verified its effectiveness in promoting Arabidopsis germination.

name: HiZJU-China
title: UNICO-fuel
abstract: UniCO-Fuel aims to address future energy challenges in Mars exploration by developing a light-controlled, sustainable aviation fuel bioproduction system based on in-situ Martian resources. Using abundant atmospheric CO₂ and solar energy on Mars, we builds a green conversion route from CO₂ to methanol and then to epi-Isozizaene (EPI), a high-energy-density aviation fuel. CO₂ is first converted into methanol through photocatalysis, and the methanol is then transformed into EPI by engineered Pichia pastoris. Compared with conventional fuels, EPI offers higher energy density, improved safety, and better adaptability to extreme environments, providing reliable power for future Martian drones, aerial platforms, and even base facilities. To enhance production efficiency, UniCO-Fuel introduces a light-controlled CRISPRi system to dynamically balance cell growth and fuel synthesis, while auxotrophic containment, suicide switches, and radiation-protection strategies ensure stable and controllable operation on Mars.

name: KAUST-KSA
title: SHIHAB
abstract: SHIHAB is a space biotechnology platform designed to enable on-demand therapeutic production in extraterrestrial environments. The system utilizes a set of robust microbial chassis (Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Pichia pastoris, and Bacillus subtilis) engineered for enhanced resilience to radiation and other stress factors to which cells are exposed in space. These organisms are then modified to synthesize a library of therapeutics and other proteins selected based on the needs of astronauts during long-duration missions. The platform is integrated into a custom-designed bioreactor created for operation under space conditions, enabling reliable, autonomous, and scalable production of essential proteins. SHIHAB aims to reduce dependency on the conventional supply chains and support sustainable human presence beyond Earth.

name: LZU-Northwest
title: Sybio-Gutweaver
abstract: Sybio-Gutweaver uses Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) to explore intestinal radioprotection and repair. We investigated melanin’s biological protective mechanisms and produced DHICA-rich melanin with enhanced free-radical-scavenging activity. We also plan to engineer EcN to secrete L-lactate to support the recovery of damaged cells and the gut microbiota. To support intestinal applications, we designed a controllable colonization module, a lactate concentration monitoring system, and an arabinose-dependent safety system. By bringing antioxidant activity, barrier-recovery support, and bacterial regulation into one design, Sybio-Gutweaver provides a foundation for further synthetic biology research into intestinal radioprotection.

name: NMU-China
title: StellaCista: A Resource-Recycling Co-Culture Platform for Space Nutrition and Flavonoid-Based Wellness
abstract:
Far from Earth, supplies dwindle. In The Martian, Mark Watney grows potatoes to survive. His ingenuity sparked our question: could astronauts also grow ingredients to support their health? 
StellaCista explores this possibility through a closed partnership between engineered cyanobacteria and yeast. Cyanobacteria use light to capture cabin CO₂ and supply sucrose to yeast, which uses this carbon and nitrogen recovered from treated wastewater to produce protein-rich biomass. Light-controlled pathways also enable yeast to produce candidate flavonoids for potential support against bone loss, sleep disturbances, and radiation-related damage. Both microbes contribute to nitrogen recovery, while space-adaptation and biosafety strategies support controlled operation. By turning recycled resources into nutritional support and on-demand products, StellaCista moves toward a living pharmacy for deep-space journeys.

name: NUS-SPS
title: Astro-Engineered Guardian of Interface Surfaces (AEGIS)
abstract:
Astronauts aboard the International Space Station (ISS) rely on the Water Processor Assembly (WPA) to recycle onboard wastewater. However, harmful bacterial colonies often form thick biofilms in hard-to-clean areas of the WPA. Their inevitable dislodgement clogs valves and filters, posing health risks to the crew. Current chemical and mechanical mitigation methods struggle to eradicate the issue.

We propose an alternative solution: using an engineered bacterial strain to out-compete native space strains. Our team will engineer a non-pathogenic strain of Bacillus subtilis and test its ability to competitively exclude biofilm-forming Escherichia coli. To prevent our engineered strain from causing similar clogging, an optogenetic switch will be linked to biofilm-thinning genes, allowing external light to control biofilm growth on demand. We hope that using ecological competition as a biofilm management strategy will be an effective solution on future space missions.

name: SZU-SIAT China
title: Friskoli: Engineering Bacterial Chemotaxis for Degradation under Microgravity
abstract: In microgravity, buoyancy-driven convection weakens and diffusion carries most of the local transport, limiting contact between microbes and solid substrates. Friskoli asks whether chemotaxis can close that distance. We engineer E. coli to carry cellulase on its surface and to sense cellobiose, the sugar that cellulose breakdown releases. Cells swim up the gradient and bring their enzymes to the material, using cellulose as our demonstration substrate. So far, we have built six strains with the chb promoter replaced on the chromosome (four of which grow clearly on cellobiose), a chemotaxis model and simulator, the Friskoli-CAD design software, a microfluidic measurement system with AI tracking, and the Space Material Atlas. In our model, visits to the material last about 2.5 times longer; our next experiments will test whether living cells show the same benefit. Crucially, this same cell-and-enzyme system is also suited for processing lignocellulose waste on Earth.

name: UFlorida
title: Computationally Optimized Space Monitoring and Omni-Sensing System
abstract: Long-duration spaceflight poses significant challenges to astronaut health, including accelerated bone and muscle loss, weakened immune function, and heighted physiological stress. Monitoring these responses is essential for maintaining crew health during extended missions. Here, we present a biosensing platform starting from computational design of the synthetic binders all the way to measuring their performance against key biomarkers. Using RFdiffusion 3 and BindCraft, we designed de novo binders targeting osteocalcin, a marker of bone turnover, and PD-L1, a protein involved in immune regulation. Candidate binders were prioritized using AI-based predictions and evaluated through AMBER molecular dynamics to teach our Model what features contribute most to binding affinity, leading to better design. Selected candidates were expressed in Escherichia coli, purified, and assessed experimentally for binding activity. This integrated computational and experimental workflow supports the development of a compact biosensor for space capable of monitoring astronaut physiology with limited laboratory infrastructure.

name: Uni-Padua-IT
title: C.O.S.M.I.C. (Cyanobacterial Oxygen Supply for Martian Inhabitant Complexes)
abstract:
C.O.S.M.I.C. addresses two bottlenecks of crewed Mars missions: oxygen production and perchlorate contamination of water. To tackle both in a single chassis, we chose the cyanobacterium Nostoc sp. PCC 7120, which photosynthetically generates oxygen from ambient CO₂. For perchlorate remediation, we evaluated endogenous nitrate reductase (NarB) activity and designed a heterologous pathway expressing perchlorate reductase (pcrABD) in micro-oxic heterocysts alongside chlorite dismutase (cld). To withstand Martian radiation, we integrated pprA from Deinococcus radiodurans, enhancing double-strand break repair.
Navigating this non-model host, we developed ReTIsigner, an open-source codon-optimization tool for non-standard chassis, and designed an inducible kill switch satisfying planetary protection guidelines. To eliminate invasive sampling while quantifying both dissolved and gaseous fractions, we engineered a non-invasive acoustic oxygen sensor.
Together, these modules form a ‘green lung’ for Mars: one organism that breathes in Martian CO₂, neutralises the  toxic perchlorates, and gives back breathable oxygen, measured without ever opening the vessel.
